Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True was filmed at Disney World and mostly at night. Yes, this new Hallmark movie was filmed at Disney World and at night. So, while the experience was magical, the cast and crew of this project on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule kind of had to turn into vampires to survive. With that in mind, I had to ask the movie’s star, Lacey Chabert, and her colleagues what exactly it was like to film in the most magical place on Earth during the hours of the day when most people are fast asleep.

While working in the parks after hours must have been an exciting prospect for the cast of Holiday Ever After, in practice it took a bit to get used to it. They were working through the night instead of the day, and according to Philip actor Travis Van Winkle, it took a second to adjust to that:

It takes a second for your whole body to adjust to that, but once you do, you become a vampire. And it's kind of nice being awake at four in the morning, and you're just wide awake, and you know, excited to film a scene. And then to watch the sunrise every morning at Disney World when no one's in the park. I mean, it was very surreal that happened every night, every morning.

Sam actor Bryce Durfee and producer David Wulf also brought up how they kind of felt like vampires making this movie. Durfee specifically said that staying awake sometimes was legitimately hard, and that is what led to this back-and-forth:

Executive producer Jennifer Aspen made it very clear that what these actors pulled off with these night shoots was “pretty exceptional.” That’s because, not only were they working on vampire hours, they also had to make sure everything got done before the sun came up and the crowds came in.

To that point, Wulf said that behind the scenes they were “communicating with every element of the parks” to make sure they got the most “amazing moment for Hallmark” without “interfering with the guest experience.” Meanwhile, while they were capturing all of that, the cast also got to experience the magic of Disney World.

Thankfully, the cast aren’t really vampires, and they could see the sunrise each morning on set (which, again, was Disney World). Lacey Chabert, who plays Lindsey in the movie, told me that was her favorite part of these night shoots too. After saying the parks were “magical” during that time, she also said:

My favorite moment was when we would finish our night shoot, then we would shoot some daytime things early in the morning, seeing the park open. The music starts. They make an announcement. Rope drop happens. People run in, and it's just this infectious excitement and joy. And I hope that all of that comes through the movie. I know that it does.

The Mean Girls actress also explained that those magical feelings were there as they were getting ready for their night shoots, too. That’s because, as they were getting ready, the parks were preparing to close, and Magic Kingdom’s fireworks would be happening:

Yeah, and our base camp was in the parking lot of Magic Kingdom, and usually our call time was about 9 o'clock, so we could watch the fireworks from the makeup trailer. I mean, once in a lifetime.

Actors get to have surreal filming experiences all the time. However, getting ready while the fireworks go off is seriously iconic.

Taegen Burns (she plays Kiera) also used the word “magical” to describe this whole experience too. She explained that despite the “wonky hours,” getting to be in the parks without other people was “incredible.”

So, now that I’ve quoted so many positive adjectives the cast used, it’s clear that feeling like vampires while filming this entry on the 2026 TV schedule didn’t bother them much. And if it did, the magical nature of being at Disney World made up for it.

Now, to see what they made during the wee hours of the night in the most magical place on earth, you can catch Holiday Every After on the Hallmark Channel on Saturday, November 28 at 8 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Hallmark+ or with a Hulu or Disney+ subscription.

#3419. Mario, Pikachu, And Other Gaming Icon Balloons Won’t Be Flying This Thanksgiving

New York City is no stranger to bad weather, be it blazing-hot summers, snow-packed winters, or fierce windstorms. Unfortunately for countless families who have made it a holiday tradition to turn on the TV and watch giant totems of pop culture sail in the streets of the great city, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been officially delayed due to a forecast of rain and windstorms--a first in its 100-year history.

In recent years, gaming icons have become more and more prominent during the parade. Beginning in 1993, a balloon of Sonic the Hedgehog marked the first game character to float among the procession. Since then, more characters have joined the festivities, including Mario, Pac-Man, Pikachu, and even Red the Angry Bird, among others.

However, those who have followed the history of Macy's balloons know that the mix of bad weather and massive, floating objects can result in genuine danger for balloon handlers, bystanders, and objects on the streets. Rather infamously, Sonic's 1993 appearance was marred by an incident where the balloon got stuck on a lamppost, popping the balloon and injuring two bystanders.

Other balloon bursts have proved even more catastrophic, with a series of mishaps in 1997 leading to a Cat in the Hat balloon causing injuries that left a woman comatose for days. Since then, more emphasis has rightfully been put on safety.

While it might be disappointing to not be able to point at the TV and go "Mario!" with your younger cousins around the TV tomorrow, the balloons will get a chance to fly on Saturday starting at 8:30 AM ET, when the weather is likely to be significantly less awful. You can find other ways to fill the time--but maybe ask your relatives first if it's okay to let the kiddos watch you play GTA 6.

#3418. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#3417. Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse

For the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Theft Auto III, the series began giving players the freedom to wreak havoc across satirical renditions of US cities. It was an amazing technical feat that only grew more impressive with each subsequent Grand Theft Auto game—and harder to appreciate the more those cities were filled with dick jokes and sex workers.

This, for the most part, suited Grand Theft Auto’s publisher just fine. What business did the company have calling itself Rockstar Games if it cared what a bunch of prudes thought?

But with Grand Theft Auto VI, something has changed. And the game’s staggering launch-day revenue—$3.79 billion—suggests that this change was a welcome one.

Rockstar has executed an astonishing about-face in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing to build a game around a couple depicted with aching sincerity—from their car-boosting meet-cute to the desperate stickups they commit, with the player’s help. Jason Duval (played by Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) are a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, out of options and on the run, hoping they can land a score big enough to turn things around.

This earnestness is new for Grand Theft Auto, which historically has had a deep love for pushing buttons. (Its sister series, the Western Red Dead Redemption, has less of a problem with heart-on-the-sleeve storytelling.) Lucia, especially, is new. She’s the first woman you can play as in the series, and by the transitive property, she’s also the first woman that Grand Theft Auto has ever had to take seriously. Doing so changes the entire shape of the series.

Until now, Grand Theft Auto has never really thought much of women. True, the games have never thought much of anyone; Rockstar traffics in a nihilistic comedy that lies somewhere between South Park and a Verhoeven film, a dim view of the United States where everyone sucks. But women, usually, have sucked the most. They’ve been the butts of countless jokes; in the Grand Theft Auto universe, they’ve been nags and drags and sex workers secondary to the men that the games were about. Grand Theft Auto III, a game that barely has a plot, begins with main character Clyde’s girlfriend betraying him after a heist, shooting him and calling him “small time” before running off with the take. It doesn’t get much better from there.

So yes: Lucia is a huge pivot for the series, especially because Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t trust players with her right away. After a brief prologue in which a desperate stickup goes wrong, Lucia is sent to jail and players begin the game as her boyfriend Jason Duval. In addition to doing odd jobs for a small-time crime boss (Stephen Root) and hanging out with your pal (Bobby Moynihan), players have to choose: Are they going to be a good boyfriend? Rockstar Games know they might be making a big ask of their audience, so they slow-roll it. Before Lucia gets out of jail, the game suggests to the player, maybe fix the stairs? Or get a haircut? Buy her a necklace?

In the days since the game came out, many have noted how amusing it is that Grand Theft Auto VI has made caring about your girlfriend one of its first challenges. The game’s “Lucia will appreciate this” notification is its first viral meme, and the source of both incel crashouts (“woke slop … so obvious it was made by women”) and earnest appreciation. (One of the first clips to spread online was of streamer Stable Ronaldo painting Jason and Lucia's bedroom one color before recoiling in horror: What if she hates that shade?)

Lucia is a destabilizing event not just for gamers, but for Grand Theft Auto—a damning yet fascinating example of gaming culture’s priorities on its biggest stage. GTA has always been a series of warring ambitions: violent Rube Goldberg machine, Karl Ove Knausgaard–esque obsession with quotidian details, and thrilling Hollywood blockbuster all in one. These disparate aims are often in conflict with one another, and one way to read the series’ heretofore exclusively male focus is as an attempt to thread this needle. By tossing all of its commentary under the carpet of “satire," Rockstar can also use a veneer of meanness to argue that the games’ misogyny is actually an intentional lambasting, much like everything else in GTA.

But taking a woman seriously, and making her colead with a male character, requires an entire rethinking of what Grand Theft Auto is. “It’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell,” Grand Theft Auto VI codirector Rob Nelson said when asked by The Guardian if this is the first Grand Theft Auto to encourage empathy from players. “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”

This is an extremely roundabout way of saying that, in this Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar asks gamers to grow up—and punishes them with narrative consequences if they don’t take the game up on the offer.

The funny thing about Grand Theft Auto VI’s gamified empathy is that, like everything else in a video game, it has to teach the player how to accomplish that goal. The game does this through prompting players to do chores, but also through Jason’s characterization. Throughout the game, Rockstar has to convey what its writers believe a well-adjusted man looks like—or at least what constitutes a man well-adjusted enough to earn the respect of a woman like Lucia, who walks out on him when he tries to exclude her from some of his more dangerous criminal activities.

To that end, there are an abundance of moments in the game where Jason demonstrates the virtues of being respectful and maintaining boundaries, several of which are a departure from GTA series norms. There are no sex workers in the game anymore (though there are strip clubs). While Jason and Lucia can break up depending on the player’s choices, there are no other options for committed or casual romance.

The money you steal is ostensibly for Jason and Lucia to use together: so they can get away and start over with their young son, who’s currently entrusted to a relative. Casual conversations between strangers players meet on the road make Jason’s respectful nature both a point and a punchline. There’s one man who’s looking for his missing wife after a night of partying. When he starts to brag about her sexual dexterity, Jason interjects to say, “Hey. Let’s draw a line, bud.”

In some ways, this is all rather embarrassing—though in a different way than the weapons-grade sexism of Grand Theft Autos past. One ought to feel a twinge of shame while marveling at any entertainment franchise for including a woman. Yet Grand Theft Auto VI is being graded on a curve. It has a near-perfect Metacritic score in large part for its depiction of Lucia, and for Jason’s relationship to her. The context speaks to a state of arrested development, both in Grand Theft Auto and in big-budget games writ large.

None of this changes the fact that Lucia really is one of the most well-realized video game characters in a digital city unlike any other. But perhaps her inclusion is less an apology for GTA’s past, and more of a concession to how out of step the series had become with the culture. Because if you’re meant to have empathy for one character, the natural next question is, “Well, what about everyone else?"

Rockstar’s maniacal pursuit of verisimilitude goes a long way here. The game’s animations are so realistic that in GTA VI, shooting unarmed civilians is legitimately unsettling. It’s also disincentivized by a “criminal profile” rating that will mark your character “irredeemable” if you engage in too much wanton violence. (This is not a “game over”—it merely locks players out of achieving a happy ending unless they restart from before their murder spree.) These sorts of limits have become another reliable source of outrage directed at the game, with rage baiters drumming up controversy over Rockstar’s decision to, for example, not permit players to shoot up a nightclub.

This is the tricky reality of encouraging empathy for “those who want to,” as Nelson put it. Rockstar has certain intentions, but so do players—and managing both is the great challenge of making any video game. Empathy is a shock to GTA’s system and to the audience alike.

Replicating humanity with computer software is a daunting and costly task, and one that only Rockstar seems to have the limitless resources to pursue. Those resources—the luxury to work as long as necessary to complete Grand Theft Auto VI, and the obscene amount of money it cost (our only solid figure is “less than $1.5 billion”)—are rapidly dwindling in the video game business, as all available tech funding is vacuumed up by AI companies and private equity loots what’s left. Grand Theft Auto VI may very well be one of one: the most expensive game ever and the last of its kind, the peak of Rockstar’s ambition and also of every big-budget video game. Here, at the end of everything, the biggest of video games has finally decided that it’s time to try empathy. And for a woman, even, should gamers choose (and not all will).

It’s a bit of an indictment of the billion-dollar video game industry that the most expensive game in history is also the first major game to commit to a realistic heterosexual relationship. Grand Theft Auto VI deserves many of the accolades it instantly garnered upon release, but the nature of its accomplishment is not yet fully understood. It’s possible that what Rockstar has built is less a monument to video games’ potential than a magnificent funeral pyre, a testament to how things might’ve turned out if Rockstar’s priorities—and those of everyone chasing after its vision of what video games could be—were just a little bit different.

#3416. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

While the fifth Toy Story gave us more insight into Jessie, it also gave us an insane Buzz Lightyear moment that was "heaven" for Tim Allen. The actor is known for his ad-libbing, both in his stand-up and in his sitcoms. Some of his best bits and impressions have made it on screen, and this goes for the toy-centric franchise as well. So naturally when the actor returned for the fifth movie, he saw an opportunity to improvise, but the Toy Story animators hated to see him coming.

Allen stopped by The Tonight Show to dish on all things Toy Story 5, and even answered Jimmy Fallon’s questions about that Buzz Lightyear army moment. The actor was totally on board with voicing 50 characters, but he admits that his excitement received mixed reactions from the animators:

The problem with a comedian is that I’m in there doing bits. I’m talking to a foam ball. ‘Cause there’s no other actors, you know? So I’m doing this whole thing and every time you ad-lib in a Toy Story movie, the people have two reactions: ‘oh, that’s funny,’ and next is, ‘darn it.’ Because they’ve already animated some of it, so if I ad-lib they gotta go back and re-do it. So they don’t really like it, but they do like it.

The actor has been playing the character since the first Toy Story in 1995, and has given Buzz a specific voice that can be "deceptively hard to capture" for writers. So Allen gives the character a little something extra that has paid off in his favor, especially since we can thank the actor for an iconic moment:

The one I did that I loved. He said, ‘You are a toy!’ And I shut - I said, ‘You are a sad strange little man and you have my pity.’ And that was an ad-lib. They went, ‘Oh God, that’s good. Oh…’

It’s hard to imagine Toy Story without that moment. Though I can see how that would be frustrating for the animators. Ironically one wish that Allen had nearly came true. He has admitted that he wanted more Buzz, as he felt the character didn't have much in prior films. Allen has jokingly said this way people won’t remember “a fabric cowboy.”

In fact, the actor almost got his wish as Toy Story 5 nearly didn’t have Woody at all. Though we did get a sweet reunion between the pals that would have been missed. While voicing so many parts at once sounds intimating, that’s not how Allen saw it:

I was in heaven, because there were 50 of me. So they run out, and then he goes, ‘We gotta go this way. We’re Space Rangers.’ The guy at the front. So I ad-libbed the two in the back. I wanted to go, ‘Why is he the leader? How come I can’t be leader?’ The other one goes, ‘Because he’s a Space Ranger and we’re all Space Rangers.’ And then he went back and forth. ‘I see no sign of intelligent life anywhere.’ ‘I see no…’ And I’m laughing my ass off in the studio. The window people are going, ‘No.’ We didn’t get one ad-lib in that thing.

However, this wasn’t the first time we’ve seen a multi-Lightyear performance. There was a moment in Toy Story 2 with several Space Ranger toys on the shelves in Al’s Toy Barn. Then we spent some time with an alternative Buzz who temporarily took our Buzz’s place. Though we hadn’t seen a multi-toy arc quite to this extent, which was everything Allen wanted it to be and more.

It’s unknown whether we’ll see another Toy Story, or if Allen (or Hanks) would return for a sixth, but a time existed when the third was going to be the last. As long as the story is there, and a chance to improv multiple Buzz Lightyears, I think the actor can easily be swayed back to the sound booth.

#3414. Jessica Chastain's 2026 Neo-Western Is A Surprise Streaming Hit On Netflix

"Heartland" is written and directed by Shana Feste, whose last project was the Prime Video supernatural horror film "Run Sweetheart Run." Prior to that, Feste made her directorial debut with 2009's "The Greatest" before helming the 2010 music drama "Country Strong." That one starred Gwynyth Paltrow as a recovering alcoholic country singer, and with "Heartland," Feste once again gives us a hard drinkin' songstress with a self-destructive streak. This time, however, she's out for justice.

Chastain's Misty Jones, as it were, is a former country music legend who's led a secluded life in Georgia ever since leaving her singing career behind. But when her niece Charlie Heart (Carter Faith) disappears, the so-called "Queen of Mean" returns to Nashville, Tennessee, to uncover the truth about what happened. But as she embarks on her quest, she uncovers a side of the city she's never seen and is forced to confront her past. Sounds alright, doesn't it? Well, Netflixers are absolutely loving Chastain's quest for justice.

"Heartland" is a strange mix of mystery thriller and noir scored by a country soundtrack that features original music from Carter Faith, who also happens to be a real-life country music star. Shana Feste appears to have taken some cues from a number of Taylor Sheridan shows in that regard, which has proven out to have been a wise move — at least, if the Netflix viewing figures are anything to go by.

"Heartland" hit Netflix on November 13, 2026, and became an instant hit. The film debuted at the top of the English movie list with 7.3 million views, finishing its first week at number two on the global movies charts with 14.8 million views. Since then it's been smooth sailing for "Heartland," according to FlixPatrol.

In point of fact, the film has remained in the top 10 in the United States for the last 10 days, hovering around the number one and two spots before dropping to number five on November 22, 2026, and number six as of November 24. But that's just part of the story, as "Heartland" is also a global hit. The film was a top 10 movie in 89 countries during the week of November 11 to November 22, 2026, and is still charting in 78 countries at the time of writing. It even hit number one in Australia and New Zealand in its second week on Netflix. All in all, then, that's a pretty good showing for "Heartland," which otherwise received mixed reviews from critics.

Writer/director Shana Feste told Texas Monthly that her aim with "Heartland" was to subvert established norms of the thriller, crime, and action genres. "We have this very established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men," she noted. "But we are not so generous with our female characters." Feste went on to describe the experience of creating Misty Jones as "incredibly freeing," due to the fact this was a character "that did not organize her life around being liked or desired." That certainly makes for a compelling protagonist in the film, and Jessica Chastain does a solid job of rendering the "Queen of Mean" in all her damaged glory.

Sadly, that only amounted to a less than impressive 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is five percentage points higher than the audience score. David Rooney of The Hollywood Reporter couldn't help himself when he described Feste's latest as "Country Weak," echoing the sentiments of The Guardian's Adrian Horton (who opined that "Heartland" "seems more destined for background music than a hit"). Nick Schager of The Daily Beast, on the other hand, thought the film managed to "offset its predictability with knockabout ferocity," and William Bibbiani of TheWrap liked it enough to hope it becomes "the first in a long, long series." With the viewership being what it is, that might just turn out to be the case.

"Heartland" might not be the best thriller Netflix has to offer, then. But it's not without its charms and comes with the Netflix audience seal of approval.

#3413. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

#3412. Why Quentin Tarantino Didn't Direct Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth."

If it looks like a Quentin Tarantino movie and talks like a Quentin Tarantino movie, you'd usually find yourself watching a Quentin Tarantino movie. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is the rare exception to that rule, however. After "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" debuted in 2019 and was heralded by many as the filmmaker's best movie yet, whispers of a continuation soon grew to a deafening noise. Tarantino then went and wrote a book based on the events of the film in a sort of reverse-adaptation situation. He subsequently spent months talking up his intentions to direct a since-shelved project called "The Movie Critic," which would've starred Brad Pitt reprising his role as Cliff Booth. But after that fell apart, David Fincher eventually came on board to direct Tarantino's script for "Cliff Booth."

After having finally seen the highly-anticipated sequel for ourselves, we (and many others) were left with even more questions regarding why Tarantino ultimately decided to sit this one out rather than sit in the director's chair himself. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a solid enough spiritual successor, albeit one where Fincher and Tarantino's unique (and wildly different) sensibilities seem to clash more often than complement. And the snappiness of the dialogue, tone, and rhythm and pacing certainly feel indebted to the quintessential Tarantino style most of us know and adore.

So, with all due respect to a legend like Fincher, was there ever a world where Tarantino had simply directed this himself? It's a complicated question with no easy answers, but below, we've rounded up a complete timeline of events — to the best of public knowledge, of course. So, here's why Tarantino's "Cliff Booth" instead became a Fincher/Tarantino joint.

It all began, as it so often does in this business, with a project that wasn't to be. In 2023, "The Movie Critic" was breathlessly announced as Quentin Tarantino's 10th and final directing gig — a self-imposed limit that the ever-opinionated artist decided to stick to, no matter what. And while rumors initially suggested this might have been based on the life of prolific writer and critic Pauline Kael, it was later revealed that this would've been an original story taking QT's usual fast-and-loose approach to fact and fiction. All seemed ready and raring to go ... until Tarantino appeared to rethink his approach (following rewrites that delayed production) and dropped the project altogether.

But Hollywood just loves a comeback story, and this wasn't the end of the line. In 2025, news broke that Fincher would be directing a sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" focused on stuntman extraordinaire Cliff Booth. It didn't take much brain power to connect the dots between the two film ideas, leading to much informed speculation that Tarantino reworked his idea for "The Movie Critic" into what turned out to be "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." For his part, Tarantino spoke to The Hollywood Reporter in 2025 and denied that Cliff was ever going to appear in "The Movie Critic." Of course, this contradicts other accounts claiming that a sort of cinematic universe may have been in the works. We'll likely never know the full behind-the-scenes story.

Did we receive the next-best outcome in its place? A Fincher/QT dream team has been years in the making, after all. Still, we can't help but wonder about what might have been.

For better or worse, what's clear is that "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" seems fated to divide viewers. There are those who feel David Fincher's involvement as director meshes beautifully with Quentin Tarantino's skills as writer, leading to a final result that's even more than the sum of its mighty parts — akin to what Fincher pulled off in his collaboration with Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Network," for instance. But there are others who feel that, while the tension between their particular styles and worldviews makes for dramatically interesting material, the push and pull between Fincher and Tarantino ultimately proves too unwieldy.

Yes, I happen to fall into that latter camp (if you haven't guessed as much already), and it's tough to reconcile the movie we have with the hypothetical version it could've been. To be fair, the evidence is fairly plain to see. Where "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is overflowing with warmth and nostalgia and a poignant perspective of time passing us by (and, okay, a whole lot of gratuitous violence, too), "Cliff Booth" stands out for how emotionally distant and cold it feels in practically every scene ... outside of Cliff's flirtations with Elizabeth Debicki's Karen Crosby or bonding moments with father Gus (Peter Weller), at least.

In the hands of Tarantino alone, it's fair to wonder if he could've brought a much-needed sense of fun and verve to the action that seems oddly missing in "Cliff Booth." What we ended up with is something caught between a Fincher and Tarantino film. Instead of half of both, wouldn't it have been more satisfying to get all of Tarantino?

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in select theaters.

#3411. This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently

This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

“Most important to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and important for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”

Surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have shows that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”

“I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” says O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”

The first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different shows practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

For O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s important to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

This is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby says. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best."

Getting to be a part of a Hallmark movie that intertwines romance and the magic of Walt Disney World is incredibly cool all on its own. However, when you’re Patrick Renna and you get to play Skipper in the 2026 TV schedule's Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True, you also delight in the joke-telling that comes with getting to take over Walt Disney World’s Jingle Cruise.

It’s heartwarming to watch The Sandlot star put on the Jungle Cruise uniform and don a Cast Member name badge as he gets the once-in-a-lifetime experience of being the boss of his own ride vehicle. He's joined a very exclusive club that few actors will ever be a part of, and I loved seeing him do what Frozen star Josh Gad did as part of a YouTube series where he takes on Cast Member jobs. Honestly, it made my heart grow watching Renna steer the cast through the attraction. Check out the clip for yourself:

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel)

Now, this was done for the film Holiday Ever After. Its star, Lacey Chabert, has always been a Disney girl, so I get why she’d want to be a part of a project like this. Not only did she get to actually film a movie inside the Magic Kingdom, but she also got to stay at the resort for the entire length of the shoot. And she shared the Disney magic of it all with her co-stars.

The Jungle Cruise is one of Disney’s most iconic attractions, so getting to be on the boat as more than just a theme park fan must be better than words can describe. And for Patrick Renna, it was a dream come true that he couldn’t help but sound in awe of. In the clip, he shared:

This is every man’s dream. This is incredible. Just walking here at 6 a.m. with no one here was one of the coolest experiences I’ve ever had.

While I’ve never gotten to take over an attraction in the theme parks, I have been lucky enough during media events to walk around Disneyland and Disney World in the early morning hours before guests arrive. I even got to take a spin on the Jungle Cruise before opening, after changes had been made to the attraction. I agree with the Dugout Dads star that not only was it absolutely the coolest experience, but also one that I’ll never forget.

If you know anything about the Jungle Cruise, chances are that you’re also familiar with the “back side of water,” as you get to see the reverse side of the waterfall. Whether it’s the classic version or the Jingle Cruise holiday edition, Jungle Cruise puns are the most important part of the experience, so it was delightful to see Patrick Renna get in on that as well.

All of this just makes me even more excited to watch this Hallmark Christmas movie release that seems to really embrace the holidays at Walt Disney World. If you're in the same boat (see what I did there), you can catch Holiday Ever After on the Hallmark Channel on Saturday, November 28 at 8 p.m. ET, or you can stream it on Hallmark+, Hulu or with a Disney+ subscription the next day.

#3409. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Fitness Equipment

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. Personally, I've been keeping an eye on all the best deals on home gym equipment that you can snag from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30).

Whether you're shopping for cardio or strength training, whether your home gym set-up is big or small, there are major discounts on brands like Peloton, PowerBlocks, Whoop, and more. Below are my favorite fitness deals I've seen so far, and I'll keep updating this list until Cyber Monday ends.

For more health gadgets, make sure to check out the best Black Friday 2026 deals on fitness trackers and smartwatches.

If you're looking for at-home cardio, you can't go wrong with joining Peloton's extensive ecosystem. Bikes are no doubt Peloton's signature offering, and the Cross-Training series (new as of 2025) includes swiveling screens and upgraded hardware compared to the original Bikes. Sticking with Peloton for a few more deals, the brand's treadmills (which Peloton calls Treads) are also available in a newer Cross-Training version. Here are the deals I'm seeing:

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but when it comes to Peloton, not all the equipment is available on Amazon. Check the Peloton website or other retailers for all your options. (I've linked each one above to a place where you can buy it—some on Amazon and some from Peloton directly.) Refer to guides like our live blog that vet deals for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3408. How Focker In-Law Director John Hamburg Helped Ariana Grande Navigate Her Tricky Character [Exclusive]

When it comes to making a movie sequel like "Focker In-Law," the challenges faced by the returning cast and crew are distinct but dependent on those faced by the newcomers. The former have to try not to repeat themselves, while the latter have to find a way of integrating their work into an already-established milieu. This can be especially tricky when it comes to comedy, as the genre lives and dies on tone and timing. If one or both are off, it can destroy the entire proceedings.

These are the precise challenges that writer/director John Hamburg and star Ariana Grande had to deal with while making "Focker In-Law," the fourth film in the uber-popular "Meet the Parents" franchise. While returning folks like Ben Stiller (as Greg Focker) and Robert De Niro (as Jack Byrnes) could rely on their past work on the property to use as a starting point, Grande had to find a path to her own comedic voice within the film's ensemble. Not making it any easier is the fact that her role is not only key, but complex: She's Olivia Jones, the bride-to-be of Greg's son, Henry (Skyler Gisondo), yet Greg is trepidatious of anyone marrying his boy. Making things more complicated is that Olivia and Greg start off on a bad note that only gets worse, as Greg discovers her past as a former FBI hostage negotiator. This means Grande has to be both a sweet-natured love interest and a potentially conniving antagonist, which is not an easy mix.

When I had the chance to talk with Hamburg about this, he agreed that the challenge was not insignificant. Yet he also revealed how he worked with Grande to craft her character, especially in the editing room, resulting in a great new addition to the Focker saga.

As John Hamburg told me during our chat, it was not lost on himself and the others behind "Focker In-Law" that Ariana Grande had her work cut out for her playing Olivia. Yet, he explained why Grande was so uniquely qualified to handle the challenge:

"We were like, 'Oh my God, she's playing the love interest and the antagonist. What a tight rope.' But honestly, she's so uniquely gifted that I think she's the only person that could really nail that thing where you're kind of scared of her, you're intimidated, but she's also the sweetest, most loving [person]. Her smile lights up a room. Ari brings so much of that energy, but she's just a wonderful actress. So, she could play all those levels."

It turns out that Grande's ability to play multiple levels of a character dovetailed nicely with Hamburg's approach to comedy, which is less about improvisation and more about tweaking the tone and intention of a moment or scene. Hamburg explained how Grande provided him with ample material that he was able to use in post-production:

"[...] When we're filming, I try to get different levels. 'So, okay, maybe try it a little more passive-aggressive, or try it a little more hostile, or say this with a smile,' that kind of thing. And she has so much in her toolbox that she was able to give me so many levels. So, when I got to the editing room, it was like an embarrassment of riches to try while I was crafting her performance."

The wrong person playing Olivia could've sunk the whole film. Fortunately, Hamburg had the right instinct that Grande could handle it.

"Focker In-Law" is currently playing in theaters.

#3407. ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

What does “Michael Caine” sound like in the freezing cold? We’re about to find out with the just-announced release of “The Trip to the Northern Lights,” which is the reunion of Steve Coogan, Rob Brydon, and director Michael Winterbottom for what is the fifth installment of “The Trip” franchise of miniseries/movies.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio picked up the U.S. rights to the fifth “Trip” film (IFC has released all four of the other films into theaters in the U.S.) and will release it theatrically on April 9, 2027. It will have been nearly seven years since the release of the last feature, and it sees Brydon now at 60 and Coogan at 59, so we’re guessing their ages may have made their wit and appetites even more ornery since. Related Stories ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

“The Trip” movies are known for their food and travel porn as much as they are for their litany of impressions between Coogan and Brydon playing versions of themselves, but this one turns that concept on its head slightly by sending Coogan and Brydon up north, this time throughout Scandinavia, including Sweden and some islands in Norway, all in search of some other fine food and wry conversation.

The first look at the movie above sees the duo in ridiculously huge parkas in the snow as guided by some sled huskies. Try doing your best Bane impression at 10 below zero.

“We are very happy to be back on the road with IFC. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first ‘Trip’ all those years ago. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights‘ takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle,” Winterbottom said. “I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.”

“The Trip” franchise began all the way back in 2011, and since then the films have spanned trips in England, Italy, Spain, and Greece. As has been the case with all of the installments, they’ve been miniseries airing on TV in England but then edited into films for the U.S. release. The first movie made $3.9 million worldwide across several re-releases, “The Trip to Italy” in 2014 made $6.1 million, 2017’s “The Trip to Spain” made $1.9 million, and “The Trip to Greece” in the COVID-addled summer 2020 still managed to make $259K worldwide.

All four of the “Trip” movies are currently available for streaming on Sun Now, which is the streamer owned by Independent Film Company parent AMC Global Media.

“The Independent Film Company is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each new trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” said Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Vice President of Acquisitions and Production.

“Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan, and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights’ advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio.

The film is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Company and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

Executive producers are Winterbottom, Coogan, Brydon, Alex Moody, Josh Sapan, Tristan Whalley, Paul Wiegard. “The Trip to the Northern Lights” is a Revolution Films, Baby Cow, and Small Man Production in association with Sky Studios.

Deadline first reported the news of the acquisition.

#3406. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.
