#3405. 5 TV Shows To Watch If You Like Blade Runner 2099

"Blade Runner 2099" has finally premiered on Amazon Prime Video, and if you've been anxiously awaiting this entry in the storied sci-fi franchise inspired by Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" (the basis for the property that launched back in 1982 with Ridley Scott's "Blade Runner"), we've got great news for you. In his review for /Film, Bill Bria praised "Blade Runner 2099" (as was overseen by showrunner Silka Luisa), declaring that Silka "has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud new addition to the saga" and even calling the series "the best sci-fi show in years."

So, what's it about? "Blade Runner 2099," like its film predecessors "Blade Runner" and "Blade Runner 2049," focuses on the interplay between Replicants — an engineered humanoid — and Blade Runners, who are tasked with figuring out who's a human and who's a Replicant and disposing of the latter. (This is what Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard was doing, essentially, in "Blade Runner.") That's where we meet Olwen, a Replicant who's also a Blade Runner — played by Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh — and watch her team up with the human Cora (Hunter Schafer) in a post-revolution world where Replicants now control humans. As Olwen prepares to be retired and Cora pretends to be a Replicant, they look for a group of evil-doing Replicants causing chaos, allowing us to follow their adventures.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are available on Amazon Prime Video as of November 25, but what should you watch when you're finished with the series? I've got some ideas.

Despite ... diminishing returns as J.J. Abrams' show "Alias" reached its endpoint with its fourth season, I still hold this show close to my heart, and fans of the double-crossing and secret identities in "Blade Runner 2099" will definitely love this spy drama. When "Alias" opens, Jennifer Garner's Sydney Bristow is, by all appearances, juggling a high-pressure job at a Los Angeles bank with her graduate studies ... except, the truth is that she doesn't work at a bank but as a spy for what she believes is a covert wing of the CIA called SD-6. When she tells her fiancé the truth about her career and SD-6 has him brutally murdered in their home, Sydney realizes that SD-6 isn't affiliated with United States intelligence but is actually a terrorist cell that's part of a larger structure operating across the world. That's when Sydney becomes a double agent, teams up with her CIA handler (and future husband) Michael Vaughn (Michael Vartan), and works alongside the other mole inside SD-6 ... who turns out to be her estranged father Jack Bristow (a sublime Victor Garber).

The first season of "Alias?" Amazing. The second season of "Alias?" God-tier television, especially "Phase One," the mid-season stunner that secured the coveted post-Super Bowl timeslot in 2003. Season 3 is where things start to go downhill, and in this house, we don't even discuss Season 4. Still, if you want to watch a few very good seasons of a spy drama after "Blade Runner 2099," check out "Alias," which is on Disney+.

"Blade Runner 2099" is many things. "Good" is one of them. "Expensive" is definitely another. You can practically see dollar signs on the screen (the show just looks expensive, and I definitely don't mean that in a bad way). So, if you're looking for another big-budget sci-fi epic that's got plenty of seasons under its belt at this point, consider checking out the Apple TV show "Foundation." Adapted from Isaac Asimov's "Foundation" book series by David S. Goyer and Josh Friedman, "Foundation," which premiered in 2021 and stars Jared Harris and Lee Pace, takes place in a future where living beings live under the control of the Empire, led largely by clones (though it's secretly run by Laura Birn's Lady Demerzel, who controls all of the Empire's leader-clones). Pace plays Brother Day, a middle-era clone of Emperor Cleon I, while Harris plays mathematician Hariton "Hari" Seldon, who can predict the future and serves as a mentor to young prodigy Gaal Dornick (Lou Llobell).

"Foundation" is detailed, sumptuous, and again, looks expensive ... and whatever Apple is spending on this series is beyond worth it. Season 3 concluded in 2025 and the fourth season is already confirmed, so if you watch the show after "Blade Runner 2099," rest assured that there will be more "Foundation" on the way eventually.

The vibes of "Pluribus" and "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't be more different, but if you like the push-and-pull of the interplay between humans and Replicants in the latter, I bet you'll like the dynamic between a hivemind and an unsuspecting woman in the former. Vince Gilligan's first series since "Better Call Saul" reunites him with that show's lead actor Rhea Seehorn and casts her as Carol Sturka, a romance author who's understandably terrified when an alien virus turns almost every human on Earth into part of a hivemind except for her (including her manager/wife Helen L. Umstead, played by Miriam Shor). As one of 12 people immune to said hivemind, Carol is at a total loss and absolutely refuses to follow the pack, which sets up a genuinely hilarious, deeply weird, and riveting series.

"Pluribus" won Seehorn her first-ever Emmy for playing Carol (well-deserved, especially after her years playing "Better Call Saul" lead Kim Wexler), and even though the series boasts a great ensemble, it's more or less a one-woman show as Carol moves through a completely changed Earth and tries to figure out her next move. If you haven't watched "Pluribus" yet and just finished "Blade Runner 2099," check this pick out.

"Blade Runner 2099" is a great series that happens to stand in the shadow of its predecessor, owing largely to the fact that "Blade Runner" is one of the most influential and beloved science fiction films of all time. This is also true of "Andor," an exceptional science fiction series that's part of a larger universe you might be familiar with called the "Star Wars" franchise. Created and run by the great Tony Gilroy, "Andor," a prequel to the movies "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" and "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope," centers on Cassian Andor (Diego Luna), a thief who becomes radicalized against the Galactic Empire over five years and ends up serving as an agent/spy for the Rebel Alliance.

I probably don't need to tell you that "Andor" is one of the best Star Wars projects ever made (this is just established fact), but both "Andor" and "Blade Runner 2099" are given the daunting task of expanding a well-known universe in a way that doesn't feel like a stingy cash grab, and both succeed. If you haven't watched "Andor" yet, you're in for a serious treat. The show only runs for two seasons, but its sophomore outing is regarded as one of the best TV seasons in recent memory by pretty much all of its fans, and it really does pair perfectly with another legacy project like "Blade Runner 2099."

If your favorite thing about "Blade Runner 2099" is the buddy aspect (namely, the way that Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh's characters play against each other), consider another Amazon Prime Video series. Specifically, consider "Fallout," the adaptation of the blockbuster video game series that started airing on the streamer in 2024. The show, created by Graham Wagner and Geneva Robertson-Dworet (with Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy of "Westworld" among the executive producers), centers around Lucy (Ella Purnell), an individual who, like most other people in this world, lives in an underground bunker to avoid the nuclear aftermath of the Great War of 2077 between China and the United States. When Lucy's beloved father Hank is kidnapped suddenly from their home in Vault 33, she decides to venture to the surface and track him down ... and while there, she encounters The Ghoul, a former TV star named Cooper Howard who was mutated by the nuclear blast and is played by Walton Goggins.

Purnell and Goggins are an unexpectedly perfect duo, much like Yeoh and Schafer. So, again, if you're looking for a follow-up series to "Blade Runner 2099" that pairs two unlikely souls together and watches them embark on a journey, try the first two seasons of "Fallout" on Amazon Prime Video. That's also where you can find "Blade Runner 2099" — again, all of Season 1 is streaming now.

#3403. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Explains One Haymitch Detail Nobody Ever Questioned

Spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead.

It's obvious why prequels are appealing. After all, they allow you to see more of the characters you love in situations that are (hopefully) less miserable than the ones you previously saw them in. The problem with prequels is that they often offer origin stories and explanations for details that no one asked about. This is how we end up with stuff like, perhaps most infamously, the bizarre explanation for how Han Solo got his name in "Solo: A Star Wars Story."

In contrast, you have the "Hunger Games" film prequels, which actually flesh out the inhabitants and world of Panem in meaningful ways. Take "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which is good enough to get you rooting for the "Hunger Games" franchise's big bad, Coriolanus Snow, as a young man despite knowing how monstrous he eventually becomes. It also reveals how the Games themselves came to be after nearly being canceled once upon a time. Notably, these explanations feel natural and crucial to the movie's story, as opposed to coming across as forced connections to the previous "Hunger Games" films.

The trend continues with "Sunrise on the Reaping," a fantastic movie that makes Haymitch Abernathy not only a hugely important character to the overall "Hunger Games" saga but one of its saddest, too. (If anything, this film shows he should be drinking more as an older man in the prior movies.) It even turns Plutarch Heavensbee into this franchise's version of Luthen Rael from "Andor," depicting him as a revolutionary stuck behind enemy lines and burning for a sunrise he'll never see.

And on top of all of that, it gives us the last backstory we expected — one for the gap in Haymitch's teeth when he's older.

Joseph Zada does a very good job in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" as Haymitch, making the character his own to embody this particular period in the character's life. At the same time, he does capture a lot of Woody Harrelson's mannerisms as Haymitch from the original "Hunger Games" quadrilogy, including his voice. That being said, there is no denying that Zada does not look that much like Harrelson — especially with his curls and noticeable lack of a gap between his two front teeth, which is Harrelson's most distinguishable facial feature.

However, rather than relying on viewers' suspension of disbelief, "Sunrise on the Reaping" actually closes the gap (pun intended) between the two actors. In the film, Haymitch is beaten within an inch of his life right before winning the titular Games, at which point he sets off an explosion as a final act of defiance. As a result, he's knocked unconscious, only to wake up later with his wounds having been stitched shut. Even so, he looks different now, with the impact of the explosion having broken his nose and smashed his teeth

This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of Hercule Poirot's mustache getting a gritty origin story tied to the horrors of WWI in Kenneth Branagh's "Death on the Nile" film adaptation, only here, it somehow works. It's because Haymitch examining his teeth is a blink-and-you-miss it detail, as opposed to one that the movie draws heavy attention to. Thus, there's no grand score announcing this as something important (like when River Phoenix's young Indy gets his scar and hat in "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade"). Instead, it's simply showing the natural aftermath of a brutal fight.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale."

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

#3400. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finale's Most Revealing Moment Perfectly Sets Up Season 4

Warning: This article contains major spoilers for the Season 3 finale of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Well, that was anticlimactic ... or was it? For much of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, we've been bracing ourselves for the onset of open war. Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) forces, bolstered by the hordes of followers loyal to the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) in Rhûn, have had their eyes on conquering Middle-earth. Even before the Dark Lord forged his One Ring, victory seemed all but certain. And, in the finale, the arrival of the Númenórean army in support of the Elves finally appeared to give us the epic battle we've been building towards all along. Instead, Sauron opts for the most shocking choice imaginable: He takes off his One Ring, kneels before King Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), and surrenders himself to his enemies without a fight.

Unless this is your first encounter with Sauron the Deceiver, of course, it's plain to see that he has plans within plans. While the details of this particular one are left entirely off-screen (we only see him look meaningfully at the approaching army and presumably inform Tyroe Muhafidin's Nazgnagôl Theo of his intentions), there's one revealing moment that tells us all we need to know. Inspired by Elrond's wisdom (Robert Aramayo) and his insistence that death is not a curse but a gift, the Men of the West begin chanting in the language of Quenya. Sauron translates for his puzzled ally: "They're asking for death." And while Theo wants to grant their request through battle, Sauron calmly implies that he has a different scheme in mind.

With just a single exchange, "The Rings of Power" perfectly tees up what's to come in Season 4.

Did you catch the subtext dripping from Sauron's words? If not, be aware that the rest of this article will contain spoilers for what's to come in Season 4 of "The Rings of Power." For the book readers, we know it all has to do with this year's season-long interest in mortal Men. Remember that conversation between Elrond and his twin brother Elros in Episode 5, when Elros revealed that he'd chosen mortality as a human over an unfathomably long life as an Elf? Elrond couldn't understand this pivotal decision then, but he's since come to understand why the godlike Valar intended this as a "gift" rather than a "doom." Between the tragedy of surprising main character Eärien (Ema Horvath) in choosing a quick death over a life of torture, the bittersweet hopes of lovers Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Elendil (Lloyd Owen) reuniting in the afterlife, and Elrond grappling with his own grief over his brother, we've seen numerous instances proving that death need not be the worst outcome.

So, perhaps it was only a matter of time before Sauron reached a similar conclusion. Having witnessed the Númenórean soldiers publicly embrace the concept of death, as the Faithful have always done, the Dark Lord smirks to himself and promises to give them what they ask ... just not in the way they think. Indeed, as we know from the canon, Sauron's abrupt surrender is exactly what goes down in J.R.R. Tolkien's original writings. In the face of overwhelming numbers, the Dark Lord allows himself to be captured and brought back to the island kingdom of Númenór, where he immediately begins causing mischief that ends in disaster.

Yeah, you probably knew where this was headed. Ever since Season 1, "The Rings of Power" has been teasing the inevitable fall of Númenór. Like Atlantis, Rome, or any number of haughty civilizations before it (both real and mythological), this empire of Men has been doomed to be humbled from the moment Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) first washed up on their shores with Sauron (then disguised as Halbrand). Even before Season 3 ramped up the conflict between the two enemy factions fighting for control of the island, the cracks in the foundation had been very apparent. And, in a bold choice, showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay haven't shied away from that, even giving Míriel visions of a "great wave" consuming them all back in Season 1.

Well, we're now right on track for this worst case scenario. With Sauron on his way and with every intention of putting the arrogant Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) in his place, expect yet another storyline where the Dark Lord manipulates one of our main protagonists — first with Galadriel, then the Elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards), and, most recently ,Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). How, you ask? Well, it has to do with Númenór's proximity to the Undying Lands to the west. Once these Men begin looking towards the Valar with envy at their immortality, encouraged by Sauron himself, it takes very little effort to imagine Pharazôn leading his forces against these godlike beings ... and paying the ultimate price for it.

Yeah, fans are going to want to stick around for everything to come in Season 4. All eight episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 are now streaming on Prime Video.

#3397. Focker In-Law Sets A New Standard For Legacy Sequels

It's a little surprising to realize, but legacy sequels like "Focker In-Law" aren't the outliers they used to be. In fairness, legacy sequels are not a brand new phenomenon. For example, Martin Scorsese's "The Color of Money" was a sequel to "The Hustler" released 25 years after its predecessor's debut in 1961.

Yet, the "legacy sequel" is a more specific concept than merely a belated sequel. Whether intended as a soft reboot or a larger continuity pivot, a legacy sequel typically involves a perspective shift to a new (and often younger) protagonist, relegating the former leads to supporting roles. This trend arguably began with J.J. Abrams' "Star Trek" in 2009, and it was solidified by "Tron: Legacy" the following year. In fact, it's entirely possible that the latter film gave the legacy sequel its terminology.

Many more legacy sequels have cropped up since then, with most of them following this template. For a period, they were generally limited to science fiction films, including 2015's "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens" and "Blade Runner 2049" from two years later. Since then, though, the legacy sequel has moved beyond the sci-fi genre to encapsulate action ("Top Gun: Maverick"), horror ("28 Years Later"), and even comedy ("Coming 2 America").

That brings us back to "Focker In-Law," the fourth film in the "Meet the Parents" franchise. Most legacy sequels attempt to recapture (if not re-stage) the movie that started it all, and "Focker In-Law" does indeed revisit the basic premise of "Meet the Parents." But rather than having longtime star Ben Stiller pass the torch to new cast member Ariana Grande, the film keeps his Greg Focker as the protagonist. It's proof positive that legacy sequels don't always need to replace older characters and can let them grow gracefully with audiences instead.

In "Focker In-Law," the now fully-middle-aged Greg Focker has two grown children of his own, and his son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) has met the love of his life, Olivia Jones (Ariana Grande). With Gisondo and Grande being buzzy young stars, it would've been understandable if writer/director John Hamburg decided to make the film from their perspective. This would essentially be "Meet the Parents" again, only this time, Olivia and Henry would be in the position Greg was years ago when he had to impress his fiancé's father, Jack (Robert De Niro). But changing Greg from the protagonist to the antagonist could've made for a lot of easy gags and forced sentiment, and it would've been very unoriginal.

However, Hamburg instead chooses to keep the focus on Greg's neurosis and knack for making huge messes out of non-issues, which has been the comedic driving force for the rest of the franchise. As such, the premise of the film is less about Olivia fitting in (she effortlessly does so with everyone but Greg) and more about Greg coming to terms with his age, his son's adulthood, his overprotectiveness, and his self-centered nature.

In this way, "Focker In-Law" is almost a coming of age story about a middle-aged adult. It's not totally rare, but it does feel notable in a medium that primarily tries to appeal to young viewers. Hence, by instead flipping the script and placating older audience members, the film's focus on Greg feels like an extension of the franchise's themes rather than a recapitulation. After all, growing up and learning doesn't stop when one hits middle age and oftentimes meeting the parents can be just as nail-bitingly uncomfortable if you're now the parent yourself.

#3396. Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

It should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to the filmmaker’s own 2019 Oscar-winning hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has always been billed as a spinoff following the continuing adventures of his fictitious (yet still iconic) stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). But Tarantino has always loved building out his own shared and connected universe(s), and fans sure love exploring its outer limits.

“Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Manson Family, of course, and all that entails). Related Stories ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

That bent continues in “Cliff Booth,” which is rife with both out-there elements and very real references (time for that “Hee Haw” resurgence, we guess). But the film also has to follow its own series logic, which means, yes, it’s the Cliff Booth show, but hey, where are our “Hollywood” co-stars Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie)?

[Once again: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

When we first meet Cliff and Rick, the duo are long-time colleagues and best pals. As his stunt double, Cliff is tasked with doing some serious heavy lifting for Hollywood star Rick, which inevitably (?) leads them to off four members of the Manson Family. The raucous and wild violence the duo inflicts on the foursome isn’t just a fun bonding exercise for the pair. It also ensures that the nefarious group can’t go next door to enact the infamous (and very real) Tate murders. Win-win!

The film ends with an invitation for Rick to slide on over to the Tate house for a thank-you drink, presumably putting him in the path of Roman Polanski, Sharon, and all the star power they carry. “Cliff Booth” is set eight years after those events, and while Rick may have enjoyed a career upswing in the interim, his current professional endeavors have taken him far from Hollywood.

While we never see Rick in the film (despite ongoing rumors that DiCaprio might appear for a quick cameo), Cliff mentions him frequently and fondly, including telling potential paramour Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) that their professional entanglements ended when Rick got, ahem, “too fat” for Cliff to believably double him and then moved to Australia to star in the TV series “Dingo Dan.” Further details on the show are slim, but we do know it’s a Western TV show that’s proven quite popular and durable (Aussie Karen seems to like it), and Cliff makes it sound like Rick is enjoying himself. Not too bad.

By blending his two movie universes with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Tarantino got to both delight in late-’60s Hollywood magic and “save” Sharon Tate, her unborn son, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, Steven Parent, and Jay Sebring. That sort of revisionist history was the film’s buzziest twist and, as I argued at the time, the most emotional choice Tarantino has ever made in his filmography.

And while we don’t get treated to much more Sharon in “Cliff Booth,” we are granted some, in the form of a Red Apple Cigarettes commercial led by a beaming Margot Robbie, returning to her original role as the doomed actress. (The fake cigarettes are another Tarantino-verse staple, and Rick even appears in his own commercial for them during the end credits of “Hollywood.”)

In the short cameo, Sharon looks healthy and happy, and she’s clearly still enough of a star to warrant her own advertising campaign, built on her smile and her zippy shimmy. As Cliff watches the commercial at the Marina del Rey condo he shares with his dad (Peter Weller), he takes the time to stop, observe, and notably smile at the star. It’s a small grace note, and a very effective one.

One other star of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is missing from “Cliff Booth,” though. Just where the heck is Brandy?

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

The anticipated battle between these two forces then does not end up happening and instead leads to Sauron's surrender. Despite featuring less action, though, season 3's final episodes are now considered among the best in the entire series.

Season 3, episode 4, "Gundabad" has a rating of 7.7/10, which means that half of the all-time top six on IMDb are installments from this season. This is indicative of the overall reception being more positive than ever, as Rings of Power season 3 reviews led to a "Certified Fresh" 87% Tomatometer score and 63% Popcornmeter score. The critics' score is a record-high and improved significantly after debuting at a series-low of 71%. Meanwhile, the audience score is "Fresh" for the first time in the show's history.

Prime Video has already confirmed that it will be building on this success with the announcement that The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has been renewed for season 4, pre-production has begun, and filming is slated to begin in the spring. The streamer shared that season 3 reached 33 million global views in its first 12 days and is among their top 10 most-watched returning seasons of all time. It has also held onto the platform's number one spot on the worldwide chart and in more than 100 countries.

All episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power seasons 1-3 are streaming on Prime Video.

#3393. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

#3392. New Avengers: Doomsday Footage Puts RDJ's Doctor Doom Accent In The Spotlight

The geography of Earth in the Marvel Cinematic Universe is mostly similar to our own world, but it does have a few fictional countries thrown in, including Wakanda, Sokovia, and now Latveria. The home nation of Victor von Doom/Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), Latveria is sandwiched between Romania, Hungary, and Serbia in Marvel's comics, but it's generally just sort of vaguely Eastern European. That means that the role of Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" called for a vaguely Eastern European accent.

Based on what we've heard from the film's trailers so far, especially this new international teaser for "Avengers: Doomsday," Downey certainly seems to have delivered on the "vague" part. In this latest promo, Doom issues a warning that "You shall all kneel before Doom," while also conveniently acting as a bit of a hype man by name-checking some of the big superhero teams that will appear in the movie. (The Thunderbolts are missing from the list, though, possibly because Doom was confused by their branding).

New international teaser for 'AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY'.

In theaters December 18. pic.twitter.com/wTudC8pKc9

— Avengers Updates (@AvengersUpdated) November 24, 2026

Downey's Doom accent has been widely compared to the voice of ancient vampire Nandor the Relentless (Kayvan Novak) in the TV show "What We Do in the Shadows." (Nandor is also from a fictional country, Al Qolnidar.) However, in this particular teaser it's more reminiscent of eccentric German filmmaker Werner Herzog. Even Downey himself has said that he struggled to settle on an accent.

"Part of me didn't want to go Eastern European," Robert Downey Jr. explained, regarding Doctor Doom's accent, in an interview with Empire. "I had written this manifesto speech that [Doom] makes, and I laid down this voice note of him addressing his people, and I started to find it there."

Downey already appeared in 10 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies as Tony Stark, aka Iron Man, so Doom presented a fresh challenge for him: "I don't want to say Tony's like rolling off a log, but I know that swing pattern." Comparatively, the process of figuring out Doom, from superficialities like his accent to his deeper motivations, was "painstaking." The fact that the character spends most of his time — possibly the entire movie, if you believe Downey's co-star Chris Evans — wearing a full face mask presented another challenge. "Honestly, a lot of it was just the eyes," Downey told Empire, adding, "I ain't gonna lie to you. A lot of this we were just trying to figure it out ... It was a bit of an exploration."

The question of whether or not Doom will take his mask off is a major one, as Downey's face is pretty recognizable within the world of the MCU. For now, though, much about Doom is still shrouded in mystery. Fans will have to wait until "Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026, to see (and hear) more from this classic Marvel villain.

#3391. The 25 Best PS5 Games in 2026

What are the best games on PlayStation 5? Hard as it is to believe, the PS5 is — by Sony's own admission — already well past the halfway point of its life-cycle. (It's even time to start thinking about PS6.) It's fair to say that PS5 hasn't been deluged with classics, and the rate of must-play new releases is slower than it has been on previous PlayStations. But it does now have the ultimate killer app: Grand Theft Auto 6.

That aside, the PS5's library has grown to the extent that there's a lot to sort through, and new and old PS5 owners will be wondering what to play. So here’s our living list of the best video games we’ve played on the platform — influenced by the personal tastes of the Polygon team — to be updated as more games come out.

Our latest update to this list on Nov. 25 added Grand Theft Auto 6.

The Polygon staff plays a lot of video games, and everything in this list comes personally recommended by at least one of us. We determined what should be on our list of the best PlayStation 5 games by looking at the quality of each title, but also with an eye for breadth and variety — so you should find something on the list you’ll enjoy, no matter what genres of game you like, how much time you have, or what vibe you are after.

A full six years into the PS5's life, here it is: the game that finally makes sense of this console generation, and makes it all worthwhile. GTA 6 is the best-reviewed game of all time, and you don't have to spend long with it to understand why. It's a deeply engrossing world of astonishing detail, reactivity, and scope, rendered in all the seedy, dayglo glamor that can be mustered by the most expensive video game production of all time. It's a familiarly scattershot satire of modern life in America. But — and it's a huge but — it's also a game of real sensitivity and heart. The central couple of Jason and Lucia are straight-up adorable and Rockstar shows, for the first time in the series' history, a moving willingness to see the best in people. Well... some people. —OW

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Grand Theft Auto 6.

If you're craving a return to the days of Wipeout, when a PlayStation racing game was as likely to involve antigravity sci-fi craft rocketing around at hundreds of miles per hour as realistic cars, then Galactic Racer is the game for you. It also happens to be one of the most innovative racing games in a long time, a much-needed shake-up for a stale genre. It introduces a roguelite structure and build-crafting into both single-player and even multiplayer modes, while keeping it all totally coherent with a very Star Wars fantasy of racing dangerous, rickety hot rods. As a treat, there's a healthy dose of Burnout in there, too. —Oli Welsh

Read Oli Welsh's full review of Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

Here's another classic PlayStation flavor resurrected in an unexpectedly glorious way. As the latest in Bandai Namco's long-running dogfighting air combat series, Ace Combat 8 sounds like a niche known quantity. Try it, however, and you'll be pleasantly surprised again and again: by the sophistication of the controls, the variety of the level design, the meaty length of the campaign, the amazing fidelity of the visuals, and the depth and seriousness of its operatic wartime storyline. —OW

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

The PS5 generation has been a bit short on really great tactics games, but that's all changed with this superb squad strategy game from Bit Reactor, set during Star Wars' Clone Wars era. Many on the team worked on Firaxis' XCOM reboot games, and you can sure tell — this is fine-honed game design full of precision, personality, puzzle-like ingenuity, and just the right amount of unpredictability. Zero Company also makes brilliant use of its setting, compellingly painting a grunt's-eye-view of the collapse of the Republic, and assembling a squad of characters you'll really care about. Especially when you lose them forever in the default permadeath setting. —OW

Read Elijah Gonzalez's full review of Star Wars Zero Company.

It's been a long time since there was an official James Bond game, and a much longer time — almost 30 years, in fact — since there was a really great one. 007 First Light might not attain the legendary status of GoldenEye 007, but it's a very slick and entertaining blockbuster action game that's a lot smarter than it needed to be. The key is an inspired choice of developer in IO Interactive, of Hitman fame. IO's love of open-ended "social stealth" gameplay sneaks its way in between the set-pieces and rounds out a thoroughly satisfying adventure with a unique perspective on a young Bond. —OW

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

It's defiantly not for everyone, but when the planets align, Bungie's take on the extraction shooter genre can be a totally electrifying multiplayer experience. Its asymmetric PvPvE gameplay can be hard to get your head around, never mind brutally unforgiving, but for intensity and drama it can hardly be matched, and Bungie is to be commended for including interesting solo as well as group roles. On top of this, you have intriguingly deep sci-fi world-building, Bungie's world-class gamefeel — 25 years on from Halo, there are still no more satisfying guns to shoot in gaming — and absolutely stunning art direction, realising one a compellingly chilling future. —OW

Read Corey Plante's impressions of Marathon.

You can accuse this sequel to Supergiant Games' smash hit roguelike action game of overcomplicating the pure brilliance of the first Hades, and we did. But really this is quibbling with something that's very close to perfection. The combat is still crisp and thrilling, the randomized boons are still exquisitely balanced, the see-saw between progression and setback on each run is still perfectly judged, and the languid, sexy bickering of Supergiant's take on the pantheon of Greek mythology is still gloriously characterful and thirsty. Simply the best that indie gaming has to offer. —OW

Capcom has completed a swift one-two punch in early 2026 by following Resident Evil Requiem with an unexpected gem of a sci-fi action game. Like all of Capcom's best work, Pragmata is both a slick, modern blockbuster and steeped in deep, old-school video game vibes. It's a cinematically ambitious game about fatherhood and the AI threat. But also you're a dude in a spacesuit shooting robots on a moon base, eking out your resources and testing your reflexes between save points.

This is a time-honored template (albeit one that makes for a pleasant gear-change in the here and now). Capcom mixes it up with Diana, your childlike android companion, who disrupts both the storytelling and the gameplay in interesting ways. She sweetly draws the best out of the protagonist, Hugh, while potentially fooling both Hugh and the player that she's any different from the AI army they combat. And her hacking ability, which plays out as a grid-based minigame, is Pragmata's chief gameplay innovation; it blends surprisingly compelling quickfire puzzles into the third-person shooting to brilliant effect — so much so that, when you earn the ability to bypass it, you'll probably choose not to. Pragmata plays solidly, looks sharp, and most importantly, feels fresh. It's a class act. —OW

Read Austin Manchester's full review of Pragmata.

It’s a bold move, on the part of Remedy Entertainment, to actually make a decade-late sequel to a game that defined the studio, but whose ambitions it has arguably outgrown in the years since — particularly in its stunning, architectural action game Control. Might a trip back to Alan Wake’s spooky woods, so obviously haunted by the ghosts of Stephen King and David Lynch, not feel like a step back? Hardly. What Remedy created by bringing all its experience to bear on its most beloved creation is nothing short of a survival horror masterpiece, as well as a meta mystery about its own creation.

Horror author Alan is joined by a co-protagonist, FBI agent Saga Anderson, who’s investigating a case linked to Alan’s disappearance over a decade earlier. Using this dual setup — impressively, you can fluidly switch between Alan’s and Saga’s stories essentially at your discretion — Remedy works outward from the original game’s premise, twisting it into a methodical detective thriller one moment and a reality-bending cosmic horror the next. Alan Wake 2 announces the start of a new generation of blockbuster horror gaming. —OW

Read Toussaint Egan’s full review of Alan Wake 2.

One of the most exciting gaming stories of 2024 has been the elevation of Team Asobi, makers of a series of charming tech demos, to the top flight of Sony’s in-house developers with Astro Bot. Expanding on the free pack-in game Astro’s Playroom, intended as a demo for the capabilities of the DualSense controller, Astro Bot is a dazzling, full-fledged, tour de force platform game capable of standing toe-to-toe with some of Nintendo’s greatest — and it’s surely the best platformer Sony has ever released.

Astro Bot is many things at once. It’s a stunning technical showcase, from the sheen of its ray-traced surfaces to the tippy-tap of the adorable Astro’s footfalls rendered in the DualSense’s haptics and speaker. It’s a nonstop riot of invention that keeps throwing new ideas, gizmos, slapstick interactions, hilarious bosses, and tortuous challenges at you. And — with its hundreds of collectible bots dressed up as PlayStation game characters — it’s a wholehearted, even moving celebration of PlayStation history in the brand’s 30th anniversary year that takes particular care to honor the many wild creations of Japan Studio, the now sadly defunct in-house developer Team Asobi used to call home. It’s poignant to reflect that the time of such creative PlayStation games as Ico, LocoRoco, and PaRappa the Rapper is passed. But it’s joyful to realize that Astro and Team Asobi are here to keep that spirit alive into the future. —OW

Read Oli Welsh’s full review of Astro Bot.

#3390. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

#3389. Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’

“The Right Stuff” was released 43 years ago, but its spectacular aerial and outer space sequences have lost none of their power. Director Philip Kaufman’s adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s book, which traced the history of the test pilots who became the first astronauts, features immersive set pieces that are still as convincing as ever, in spite of decades of technological advancements since it was made. To revisit it via Criterion‘s new 4K UHD physical media release is to experience one of the most groundbreaking and enduring films of all time.

The new Criterion transfer was supervised by cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, who was still relatively early in his career when Kaufman tapped him to shoot “The Right Stuff.” Deschanel didn’t have many feature credits, but the ones he did have were impressive: his early work included the stunning imagery of “The Black Stallion” and two Hal Ashby movies, “Being There” and the Rolling Stones concert film “Let’s Spend the Night Together.” He would earn the first of his six Academy Award nominations for “The Right Stuff.” Related Stories Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March

Deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock shows at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire. Deschanel visited the set of “Minnesota” and stayed in touch with Kaufman, who called him around 10 years later with the offer to shoot “The Right Stuff.”

“It was a dream come true,” Deschanel said, noting that he had always been an aviation buff who loved going to air shows with his father. He also remembered that Kaufman wasn’t the only person on “The Right Stuff” who he had met years earlier. “Years before we had moved into our first house and needed some painting done, and we had a friend who was teaching in the Cal Arts theater department. He said, ‘I have this actor who’s really great who paints houses in the summer.'”

Deschanel hired the young actor and got to know him a little bit, and five years later was having lunch with his wife Mary Jo and Kaufman when Kaufman showed them a picture of the actor he had chosen to play John Glenn. “I said, ‘We know him. That’s Ed Harris. He painted our house,'” Deschanel said. “Then, coincidentally, the woman who was supposed to play Annie Glenn dropped out of and Phil cast my wife, so they ended up playing husband and wife in the movie.”

One of the great technical challenges of “The Right Stuff” was integrating archival footage of the space race with the new material being shot — one of the reasons the movie was shot in a 1.85:1 aspect ratio instead of a wider Panavision format as one might have expected for such an epic film. “We were using actual footage of NASA’s rocket launches and things like that, and they were filming in the old-fashioned 4:3 format using the full frame of a 35mm camera,” Deschanel said. “Converting that to widescreen was really impossible.”

Working in close collaboration with visual effects supervisor Gary Gutierrez (who provides a fascinating look at the film’s miniature and rear-projection work on the Criterion disc), Deschanel solved the numerous logistical problems that came with trying to make it look as though the actors were hurtling through the air at the speed of sound and beyond. Even when Gutierrez thought he had solutions that would work, they often had to be tweaked to accommodate Kaufman’s desire to make everything feel as realistic and immersive as possible.

Early attempts to use a motion-control system for the effects, for example, were discarded because the camera movement was too smooth for Kaufman’s purposes. “Phil wanted it to have some energy to it,” Deschanel said. “That changed the whole methodology.” Whenever rockets were taking off or various crafts were flying, Deschanel made sure to add some shake to the camera. “I actually gave my camera operator, Craig Denault, a black eye at one point because I was hitting the camera so hard.”

In addition to the expected challenges, there were plenty of unexpected ones as well — like the fact that Sam Shepard, who played ace pilot Chuck Yeager, wouldn’t fly. “The only time he ever went up in an airplane was when Yeager took him for a flight,” Deschanel said. “Other than that, whenever we had a mockup of an X-1 or the F-104 or anything like that, he’d make me get in and show him how it was going to twist and turn before he would get into it.” For Yeager’s scenes and many of the others, rear projection was used — meaning Deschanel had to photograph what was seen outside the pilots’ and astronauts’ windows long before the actors’ material was actually shot.

“There was a lot of complexity to all those things,” Deschanel said. “But it gave it a real energy and sense of being there. And that’s what you try to discover as you’re filming any film: what is that visual metaphor that really makes you believe you’re having the same experience the characters are having?” Creating that sense of authenticity required some unorthodox approaches, as when Deschanel had a Learjet pilot take the nose cone off of his plane and replace it with a clear dome.

“We put a camera in there with a 15mm lens, and then we were able to go up above 50,000 feet,” Deschanel said. “At that level, it’s so dark, it’s almost like you’re in outer space. Anything you could think of to find the reality of the movie, we employed.” Deschanel’s perfectionism became the stuff of legend over the years, with some people who worked on “The Right Stuff” claiming he insisted on shooting only at sunrise or sunset to get the most beautiful possible images — a myth Deschanel is quick to dispel.

“The fact is we shot all day long and had really long days,” Deschanel said. “There was one point where, just to finish up at Edwards Air Force Base, I was on for 24 hours and changed the crew in the middle. So I had a whole new crew for the second half of that long day.” That said, Deschanel acknowledges that the film’s justly famous exteriors were important to him, in part for what they represented.

“The iconic moment is when Yeager is on horseback, and he rides up and sees the X-1,” Deschanel said. “It’s like ‘The Professionals’ or ‘The Wild Bunch,’ these movies about the end of the West as new technology takes over. To me, there’s this wonderful representation of the end of an era when Yeager comes across this fighter jet. Then, of course, he flies it and breaks the sound barrier. So it’s this wonderful juxtaposition of important moments in human history, where one person does something that further advances flight to the point that makes it possible for the next generation to go into outer space. I always miss that I never got to make a Western, but in a way, ‘The Right Stuff’ is a Western.”

“The Right Stuff” special edition 4K UHD release is now available from Criterion.

#3388. Prime Video's 8-Part William Gibson Adaptation Was Robbed Of Its Chance To Be A 10/10 Sci-Fi Series

Prime Video had a short-lived William Gibson cyberpunk sci-fi series that had all the elements to develop into a 10/10 show, but its potential was never realized onscreen. Prime Video's TV show catalog features quite a few notable sci-fi series. The genre is well represented through comedies like Upload, the intense The Expanse, and other exciting genre shows.

For instance, Prime Video just released one of the most ambitious sci-fi TV shows in the age of streaming. After all, the streamer has tapped into one of the most iconic franchises of all time, Ridley Scott's Blade Runner, for the sequel series Blade Runner 2099, which is set 50 years after the last film in the cyberpunk franchise, Ryan Gosling's Blade Runner 2049.

Speaking of cyberpunk TV shows, William Gibson is often referred to as the creator of that important sci-fi subgenre. After all, his hit book, Neuromancer, is highly regarded as foundational to all cyberpunk stories that have come after it. Gibson fans can look forward to that franchise being adapted into a live-action series on Apple TV, as Neuromancer, starring former James Bond candidate Callum Turner, debuts on January 22, 2027.

Those looking for a genre show to watch while waiting for Apple TV's Neuromancer next year can find not only what stands as one of the most intricate sci-fi TV shows in recent years, but another project based on Gibson's work. The TV show in question is The Peripheral, and I still can't believe it was robbed of the chance of becoming a 10/10 show.

The Peripheral debuted on Prime Video on October 21, 2022, with eight episodes being released on the streaming service until the finale on December 2, 2022. The cyberpunk series went through one of the most disappointing arcs in the streaming age, as The Peripheral holds a strong 79% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes and an even better 85% audience score, with the show having originally been renewed for season 2 only a couple of months after its season 1 finale. By all accounts, it laid a solid foundation for what could be years of complex sci-fi storytelling.

However, due to the effects of the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, Prime Video walked back on the renewal, canceling The Peripheral in August 2023. To say that was disappointing is not enough. Gibson is known for being one of the most skilled authors in the sci-fi genre, and The Peripheral showed a lot of promise in its first eight episodes. The series had to deal with complicated elements, as its story consists of two interconnected timelines separated by 70 years, headsets that can send people's consciousness across timelines, and a fast approaching apocalypse known as the Jackpot.

There was a lot of worldbuilding to unpack in The Peripheral season 1, but the show did a mostly fantastic job at making all these complex ideas feel interesting and urgent. With impressive VFX, kinetic action sequences, sharp writing, magnetic performances, and plenty of mysteries left to unfold, The Peripheral's eight episodes looked like a clear case of a TV show that was preparing itself to get even bigger and better in its next season. This is why the show's cancellation still stings three years later, as the lasting feeling is that it was robbed of becoming a true sci-fi masterpiece.

Making matters worse is the fact that The Peripheral was packed full of talent both in front and behind the camera. Chloë Grace Moretz as Flynne Fisher and Jack Reynor as her brother, Burton, commanded the screen and were easy to connect with. T'Nia Miller's Cherise Nuland was an intense and cunning villain, and her recent showstopping performance as Jocasta in Marvel's sci-fi series VisionQuest was a reminder of what we lost. Then there is the fact that Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy, who were behind HBO's Westworld and Prime Video's own Fallout, were executive producers. The Peripheral simply deserved better.

"Avengers: Doomsday" may feel like the grandaddy of all Marvel Cinematic Universe films, but even this gargantuan production can't hold a candle to the absolute icon at its heart. In a new profile with Entertainment Weekly, the cast and crew of "Doomsday" opened up about their memories of working with Stewart, the immense legacy he leaves behind, and the unforgettable experience they had watching him on his very last day filming. To Kevin Feige, the Marvel head who was present as a lowly associate producer during Stewart's very first appearance as the mutant leader in 2000's "X-Men," the words Stewart spoke after wrapping filming on "Doomsday" feel even more poignant in retrospect:

"He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew. We didn't know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was."

"In a lot of ways, Xavier's the conscience in the movie. He has a lovely scene with Ian McKellen, who's his best friend, in the film. It's a very emotional scene about forgiveness and I think very resonant in the wake of his passing."

For his part, Kevin Feige acknowledged that he and the Russo brothers have been busy putting the final touches on "Doomsday" — including a tribute in memory of Stewart, likely in the end credits of the film. As he put it:

"We're long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us. We're looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend."

Considering similar memorials for dearly-departed figures like Leonard Nimoy, Carrie Fisher, Chadwick Boseman, and many more in recent years, don't expect a single dry eye in the house once the lights come on. "Avengers: Doomsday" will arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3386. 'Avengers: Doomsday' Is Making Sure Patrick Stewart Gets a Proper Sendoff

The late X-Men and Star Trek star will receive a special tribute in December’s Marvel blockbuster

Patrick Stewart's final on-screen performance will arrive in December's Avengers: Doomsday, and Marvel is making sure the late actor receives a fitting farewell.

Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige and directors Anthony and Joe Russo are planning to include a tribute to Stewart in the upcoming superhero blockbuster, according to a new interview with Variety. Stewart died on Oct. 29 at age 86 following a brief battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

The actor had already completed filming for Doomsday, in which he reprises his iconic role as Professor Charles Xavier for the ninth and final time. Speaking to Variety, Feige revealed that Stewart's last day on set was an emotional occasion, with the actor delivering a speech to the crew.

"He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew," Feige said. "We didn't know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was."

Anthony Russo also recalled how difficult filming had become for Stewart as he struggled with his health. Despite the challenges, the actor remained committed to delivering his performance.

"For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional," Russo said.

Although principal photography has wrapped, Feige said Marvel is now figuring out how to properly honor its longtime collaborator.

"We're long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us," Feige told Variety. "We're looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend."

The tribute will carry particular significance given Stewart's history with the X-Men franchise. He first played Professor X in 2000's X-Men, becoming one of the defining faces of the superhero series alongside Ian McKellen's Magneto. The two actors will reunite in Doomsday, with Joe Russo revealing that their characters share an emotional scene about forgiveness.

"In a lot of ways, Xavier's the conscience in the movie," Russo said. "He has a lovely scene with Ian McKellen, who's his best friend, in the film. It's a very emotional scene about forgiveness, and I think very resonant in the wake of his passing."

Stewart's death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fans, fellow actors, and gaming communities. Players of No Man's Sky, for example, began naming planets and entire star systems after the actor, with some creating virtual memorials inspired by his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on Dec. 18.

#3385. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Features A Delightful Quentin Tarantino Easter Egg

Spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" follow.

Forget the MCU. Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years. For instance: while this is never officially stated by anyone on screen, Michael Madsen's character from "Reservoir Dogs" is supposed to be the brother of John Travolta's character from "Pulp Fiction" (there was even a plan for a crossover movie, but it never happened). Beyond character connections, Tarantino also likes to drop his own fictional products into his films, and "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps this trend going.

Tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher. But Tarantino still wrote the script, and Fincher keeps the Easter eggs intact. The biggest example: Big Kahuna Burger. Early in the film, we see Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth pick up some food at Big Kahuna Burger to bring home to his dad, Gus (Peter Weller). Tarantino fans will, of course, recognize that burger joint: it was prominently mentioned in "Pulp Fiction," and we see Samuel L. Jackson's character Jules take a big bite of a burger while intimidating some crooks who are about to meet a violent end.

But wait, there's more! Another Tarantino product that shows up in "The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" are the famous Red Apple Cigarettes. Red Apples have been mentioned in virtually every Tarantino film, and they were even a part of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the film that "Cliff Booth" serves as a sequel to.

In "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton filmed a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes (believe it or not, kids, there used to be commercials for cigarettes on TV). "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps the tradition alive while also giving us a nice little callback. During one scene, we see Cliff watching a new Red Apple commercial on TV. And who is starring in that commercial? None other than Sharon Tate, played by Margot Robbie in a cameo.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" ended by literally changing history, and allowing Sharon Tate and her friends to completely avoid their tragic murders at the hands of the Manson family. "Cliff Booth" confirms that since Sharon is still alive in 1977, when the film is set, she's still out there acting, too.

#3383. Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion

It’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024. But if it feels like the black and white, silent, slapstick indie comedy still hasn’t left the cultural conversation, that’s because in all that time it has continued to quietly play in theaters and attract audiences both loyal and new alike.

Technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters. It continues to play individual screenings in a city or two every weekend. Now, though, “Hundreds of Beavers” is set to return to theaters for what is its biggest theatrical expansions to date. The film will kick off its third annual Northwoods Christmas, which will feature 130 screenings across 85 cities, with more to likely be added in the coming weeks. It came about after another fan campaign pushed for the film to come to some markets it hadn’t previously thought about or targeted such as Indianapolis and Charlottesville, and it will now play in everything from concert venues to microcinemas. Related Stories Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’ Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a new Christmas movie. The first time “Hundreds of Beavers” was re-released at Christmas 2024, which was shortly after the Blu-ray for the film became available, it brought in $118K at the box office in a month, and the producers continued the tradition in 2025.

“There’s room for a Christmas tradition with the energy of a ‘Rocky Horror’ screening,” said producer Kurt Ravenwood. “You can watch ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ and ‘White Christmas’ all you want, but for getting together with friends and family to laugh about the miserable winter ahead, ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ has them all beat.”

Each of the screenings will be preceded by a short film featuring “Bing Crosbeaver,” which they did last year, but this will be a new short with a new twist in which another character named “Conspirabeaver” will be joined by a “sinister foe,” per the release. Some of the in-person beavers in costume will be present at the screenings, and fans will also get a promotional poster for the movie. The “Beavers” team recently released a few parody posters ripping off the recent releases of “You Can See Everything,” “Digger,” and “The Devils.”

To date, “Hundreds of Beavers” has made $940,092 at the domestic box office, including another $618,014 internationally to bring its worldwide total to above $1.5 million. It’s done all this via first producing the film for just $150,000 and spending little more than $70,000 on ads, publicity, and its many roadshow screenings. It’s also been released entirely independently, starting with a run in the Midwest where the film is set before it started expanding to the coasts.

Incredibly, more than 70 percent of the film’s U.S. box office has come after “Hundreds of Beavers” began streaming way back on April 15, 2024, and it has even sold more than 20,000 Blu-Rays worldwide. It’s a rare, truly indie success story even in a day and age when many movies have pursued self-distribution strategies.

For those who haven’t had the pleasure of seeing “Hundreds of Beavers” in theaters yet, the film is about a drunken applejack salesman who loses everything and has to survive the winter by becoming North America’s greatest fur trapper. It sees the trapper wrestling and fighting with dozens of beavers and other forest animals all wearing mascot suits, with the stark black and white cinematography and creative physical stunts embracing a zany video game logic and absurd silent comedy slapstick gags.

The film is directed by Mike Cheslik and was written by Cheslik and star Ryland Tews, with the film also starring Olivia Graves, Wes Tank, Doug Mancheski, and Luis Rico.

#3382. David Fincher's Rejected Star Wars Movie Pitch Would Have Centered On Two Beloved Franchise Characters

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

His interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:

"I said, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were."

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

"Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened."

Notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:

"I said to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'"

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.
