#3361. Michael C. Hall's 8-Episode Harlan Coben Netflix Series Is An Intense Binge

Even though Michael C. Hall has been on plenty of disturbing shows over the years, Netflix’s underrated Harlan Coben series is one of the actor’s most intense series to date. Michael C. Hall has never been an actor who worries too much about playing likable or relatable characters. From the role of the predatory David Kammerer in 2013’s literary biopic Kill Your Darlings to his most famous role as a “serial killer killer” in Showtime’s Dexter franchise, the actor is entirely open to morally ambiguous roles.

This has often been a good thing, with Hall’s uncompromising portrayal of John F. Kennedy marking a high point in 2017’s The Crown season 2. Meanwhile, although Six Feet Under’s David Fisher was never a villainous figure, the hardships that he faced during the HBO drama’s five-season run also called on Hall to explore the darker sides of the human psyche at length.

While the Dexter franchise is still Hall’s most iconic exploration of a deeply disturbed but strangely compelling character, it is far from his only unmissable role as an amoral protagonist. Netflix’s underrated Harlan Coben adaptation Safe is one of the streaming service’s most intense shows based on the Myron Bolitar creator’s books, and this is thanks in large part to Hall’s mesmerizing central turn in the eight-episode miniseries.

Safe follows Hall's Tom Delaney, a pediatric surgeon who has a hard time connecting with his daughters after the death of his wife. When one of Tom’s daughters goes missing, this sparks a complex plot that exposes years of lies, cover-ups, and family secrets, all with Hall’s protagonist at the center of everything. While early reviews hinted that Safe could be Netflix’s answer to Broadchurch, critics soon noted that the Coben show was soapier and more dramatic than that darker murder mystery.

While this might sound like a condemnation, fans of Coben’s output will likely know better. Some of Netflix’s best psychological thriller shows, like Mindhunter, are dour, maudlin series with patient pacing and a bleak tone. Others, like The Hunting Wives or the five-season hit You, are campy, playful takes on the psychological thriller genre that are no less thrilling for their winking sense of humor and more outrageous tone.

Like many of the best Coben adaptations, Safe dances on the line between these two extremes. While Gone for Good, No Second Chance, The Stranger, The Innocent, The Woods, Stay Close, Hold Tight, Fool Me Once, Missing You, Run Away, and I Will Always Find You aren’t all perfect, Netflix’s Coben adaptations do all use their grounded tone to sneak in some ludicrously shocking plot twists and absurd moments.

Where shows like Mindhunter or HBO’s Mare of Easttown are grounded and realistic throughout and hits like The Hunting Wives or You abandon this in favor of self-aware fun, Safe maintains a serious, somber tone while its plot pulls off all manner of wacky and unlikely revelations. Central to the success of this tonal juggling is Hall’s performance.

Subtle and layered, Hall’s take on Tom makes the surgeon feel like a real, believable character trapped in a bizarre story, rather than a self-aware character or a soap opera protagonist. Thus, even Safe’s silliest moments still hit hard thanks to Hall’s years of practice taking larger-than-life characters in outlandish situations and unearthing their underlying humanity.

All of Netflix’s 12 Coben shows will appeal to viewers who just love a thriller full of plot twists, but some are sillier and less believable than others. In Safe, Michael C. Hall’s unmissable turn makes Netflix’s psychological thriller the perfect balance of grounded believability and gripping, unpredictable fun.

#3360. If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating new crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and launches a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

This might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. #3359. 6 Fantasy Books Better Than Harry Potter

Monsters, magic, and mayhem that will leave Hogwarts dusty on the shelf

There's no denying that Harry Potter continues to be a phenomenon. After seven bestsellers translated into multiple languages, years of extravagant midnight release parties, eight big-budget films, a stage play, and theme parks, there's still enormous hype for both the upcoming HBO television show and an all-star re-recording of the audiobooks. Clearly, there is something about the boy who lived and his world that draws people in and keeps them captivated. All of this begs one very important question, however: how good are the Harry Potter books, really?

The answer to that question is, ultimately, a matter of personal taste, but the books do have their faults, from skimming mythology and using, at best, insensitive naming conventions to treating serious issues as fodder for gags and jokes. There's also the perennial question of whether the artist can be separated from their art. The good news is that there's a lot of fantasy in the world waiting to be read. Here are six fantasy books better than Harry Potter:

Set in the same world as Percy Jackson and the Kane Chronicles (Magnus is Annabeth Chase's cousin), this book follows Magnus, an unhoused teen on the streets of Boston who discovers he's the son of Frey. After dying in battle, he becomes an einherjar and a resident of Hotel Valhalla. A Valkyrie named Samirah Al-Abbas convinces Magnus to help her stop Ragnarök.

While a fantastic adventure full of Riordan's signature charm and wit, Magnus Chase also touches on the ways so many people, including children and teens, are othered because of their gender identity, disability, housing instability, poverty, or religion​​​​​​​. This book, however, never once uses any of these topics as the subject of a joke or a reason for the characters to be cruel to one another​​​​​​​. That's not to say everyone who populates the world is perfect; they have quirks and foibles and they make mistakes. There are, of course, true villains. But the lack of casual cruelty allows Riordan to bring together a found family built on choice, mutual respect, and determination—a believable family that allows each character to explore openly and honestly what's been difficult and traumatic for them.​​​​​​​ Riordan uses impeccable research with care to create a story that pays tribute to it.​​​​​​​

The Sword of Summer is the first book in a trilogy.

Six of Crows is set in the same world as Bardugo's Shadow and Bone series. It follows a group of thieves hired to break into a heavily guarded prison to rescue​​​​​​​ a scientist experimenting with a drug that amplifies Grisha magic to potentially deadly levels​​​​​​​. The crew is, of course, a motley bunch, all of whom have dark pasts they promise won't cause complications. In the tradition of every great heist story, those pasts do, indeed, make everything a thousand times more difficult.

These are also the stories that Bardugo does best: the smaller, more intimate ones. The stories with twists and turns and complications that leave characters trapped in the prisons of their own minds. The ones that mislead and distract until, suddenly, the scales fall away and the true double-cross is staring right at the intrepid almost-heroes, ready to crush them. No Harry Potter book ever made readers hold their breath the way the conclusion of Six of Crows will.​​​​​​​ It's probably a good idea to have Crooked Kingdom, the conclusion of the duology, standing by.​​​​​​​

Blue, a girl from a family of psychics, has grown up being constantly reminded​​​​​​​ that she'll kill her true love with a kiss. That doesn't stop her, however, from befriending a group of boys from the local private school and joining them on their quest to seek out a legend: the Welsh king​​​​​​​ sleeping in the hills that surround them. Gansey, the group's leader, tells her that the first person to wake the king will get a wish.​​​​​​​ Blue accompanies the boys as they search, despite the danger and all the strange things​​​​​​​ that seem to happen when they go looking.

The Raven Boys is a marvel of atmosphere and mood. It gathers the reader in and holds them there, keeps them enmeshed in the world Stiefvater has created. Rather than bouncing around from setting to setting, it unfurls like the landscape it describes, presenting a magnificent vista that spreads wide before the reader and makes magic of what's right in front of them, accessible through their own senses​​​​​​​. It also makes magic a horror-tinged phenomenon, something to be wary of, something beautiful but dangerous. Something with a price.​.​ Like Magnus Chase, The Raven Boys blends fantasy and reality by also exploring income inequality and difficult home situations honestly but without ever shaming or humiliating the characters trapped in those experiences.​​​​​​​

There are four books in The Raven Cycle, which is currently being adapted into a series of graphic novels​​​​​​​.​​​​​​​

Christopher is not supposed to go near the water. Like many fantasy heroes, he disobeys​​​​​​​ and finds a drowning baby griffin. He saves it​​​​​​​ and is tasked with taking it back to the Archipelago, a hidden place where magical creatures are supposed to be safe. Once there, he meets Mal, a girl with a miraculous flying coat, and learns that magic is slowly dying, as are the inhabitants of the Archipelago​​​​​​​. Mal convinces Christopher to go with her on a quest to discover what's happening and to save their impossible friends.

A middle-grade book, it will be a quick read​​​​​​​ for adults and a great book to read with kids of a certain age​​​​​​​. This is also a great book for kids because, while the adults keep secrets from Christopher, his grandfather breaks the cycle and becomes a trusted adult—something that doesn't happen in many fantasy novels.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Katherine Rundell is fantastic at setting scenes, and each one comes together beautifully​​​​​​​, painting the Archipelago in bright swaths of color and incredible detail. There is a cliffhanger at the end of book one that may be a little upsetting; the good news is that books two of this planned five-book series​​​​​​​ is already out.

Bree Matthews hopes going to UNC early for a residential program will help her escape the grief of her mother's death. Her first night on campus, however, she stumbles into a demon attack and discovers a secret society whose members​​​​​​​ are descended from King Arthur's knights. When Sel, their mage, or Merlin, tries to wipe Bree's memory, he fails but unlocks abilities that suggest Bree too is a Legendborn.Initially turning down an invitation to join the group, Bree changes her mind when she discovers that a Merlin had something to do with her mother's death​​​​​​​. What she ultimately finds out is unimaginable.

Fantasy is rife with Arthurian retellings, but Legendborn is something special. The modern college setting gives the story room to breathe and allows Deonn to make some fascinating innovations with the material.​​​​​​​ The story's exploration of different magic systems keeps Bree grounded in the world​​​​​​​ even as she's discovering her powers, which is essential for her growth both as a person and within the Arthurian framework. Each of the characters in Legendborn has a role that's been assigned to them, but they also have their own desires​​​​​​​, and the conflicts and real-life stakes this interplay creates make the story that much more interesting.​​​​​​​ The exploration of grief is also important; it holds the narrative together and carries it forward, much as real grief shapes a life, especially after the loss of a parent.​​​​​​​ It influences everything that Bree does and every choice that she makes. It takes skill to pair fiction and reality so deftly.​​​​​​​

The second and third books of the series, Bloodmarked and Oathbound, are out. An as-yet-untitled fourth volume​​​​​​​ is planned.

Rui is an exorcist determined to avenge her mother's death. But one day, in the middle of a battle, her powers disappear. They reappear in Yiran, a boy from a wealthy family who would have had a perfect life if he had been born with abilities; now, suddenly, he does and as far as he's concerned, his new magic will fix everything. Nikai is a reaper whose boss, the Fourth King of Hell, has disappeared.​​​​​​​ Without the ten kings tending to their respective realms​​​​​​​, the underworld starts to crumble, and the human realm won't last much longer. So when Rui thinks she's discovered a lead on the missing fourth king and a way to get her powers back, she makes a dangerous deal.

Darker by Four builds on mythology instead of sprinkling it in where it's convenient or where it sounds good. The story reflects a deep understanding of the source material, which is truly integrated into the narrative; the legends here are load-bearing.​​​​​​​ That doesn't mean they're cited word for word, but it does mean there's a fundamental respect.​​​​​​​ The story itself is also a lot of fun while dealing with some serious topics: grief, othering, and identity. There's also the matter of the magic itself: characters who can use magic quickly discover that it doesn't save them from their responsibilities and that, sometimes, it's a greater burden than a gift. When things are broken, they can't simply buy a new wand.​​​​​​​​​Brighter than Nine completes the duology.

#3358. Blade Runner 2099 Adds A Major Twist To The Classic Voight-Kampff Test

I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe. This article discusses major plot details from all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099."

What's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant? Throughout both films, organics in this post-apocalyptic setting were able to "enjoy" their time at the top of the food chain. That all changes in Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099," the live-action story taking place after the world order has been upended and our supposed underlings have gained all the power for themselves. While Replicants were built to be "more human than human," the subtle differences between the two kinds are all but impossible to detect — on the surface, at least. But, as we know, looks can be deceiving; what's underneath is another matter entirely.

Leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head. Traditionally, the purposefully off-putting questionnaire known as the Voight-Kampff test was meant to detect whether an individual is a Replicant or not. In the sci-fi series, the rise of the Replicants and the 50 years that have passed since "Blade Runner 2049" have introduced even more changes. Enter the Index Test, an inverted form of the established quiz. But rather than differentiate between the two beings, this test is meant to detect whether the subject has developed feelings of empathy towards humans.

In Episode 5, titled "My Lord," we learn far more about this strange new setup than the show had previously revealed. All we ever saw was the unusually young human girl administering the test, the odd non sequiturs she posed to (supposed) Replicants like Hunter Schafer's Cora, and the results of whether they passed the baseline or not. But that, too, was only scratching the surface.

Of all the differences between humans and Replicants, empathy is the biggest of them all. "Blade Runner 2099" draws fairly stark lines in the sand between the two, with flesh-and-blood people now completely helpless before their bioengineered creations. But despite their physical advantages and killer instincts, Replicants' lack of a childhood means they're deficit in that crucial, compassionate emotion separating humans from all other living things. As we soon learn, however, Replicants can feel these strong feelings ... and actually fear it, too.

This is all summed up in the storyline involving Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), the young human girl we learn has been sold off into indentured servitude and indoctrinated along with many others into administering Index Tests. Episode 5 peels back all the horrifying layers, showing us Greta's training under awfully unsettling circumstances. First, she's taken through a museum exhibit explaining the purpose and history of the Voight-Kampff test, used by human Blade Runners to hunt Replicants. Now, the new status quo means Replicants use this new Index Test to police their own kind — and, as one instructor explains, prevent any "emotional contagion" crossing over from humans to their Replicant overlords.

It's a fascinating idea with some pretty serious implications for our two main characters. Michelle Yeoh's Olwen is currently undergoing some serious emotional turmoil herself, as her search for the missing Replicant and her secret lover Marek (Johnny Harris) ends in his tragic death. Meanwhile, Cora's own emotional attachments makes it only a matter of time before her human identity is made known. As a result, every time they sit down for the Index Test makes for must-watch TV.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are streaming on Prime Video.

#3356. Star Trek Officially Brings Back Captain Janeway For 60th Anniversary Celebration

It was in May 1964 that Star Trek burst onto the scene and sent the sci-fi genre into a tail spin thanks to a universe which introduced diverse characters, stories, and settings. Created by Gene Roddenberry and first premiering on television in 1966, Star Trek has now cemented itself as one of the most influential shows of all time, going on to inspire multiple spin-offs, movies, video games, novels, and more.

Now, over six decades on from its inception, Star Trek has returned an iconic character as part of its 60th anniversary celebrations, and as of 24 November, you can hear all about Captain Janeway's perilous journey home in one brand-new release which will be a must-buy for the Star Trek fans in your life.

Despite the Star Wars universe being home to many iconic characters, there is no denying that Captain Kathryn Janeway is definitely one of them. Serving as the main character in the television series Star Trek: Voyager, she was the captain of the Starfleet starship USS Voyager and had to navigate the trials and tribulations of being lost in the Delta Quadrant on the other side of the galaxy. Portrayed by Kate Mulgrew, the actor has returned to bring life to the role once more in Star Trek Timelines, a new hardcover book from DK that features 336-pages of the entire fictional universe we have fallen in love with over the past 60 years.

Not only that, but Mulgrew has provided a foreword detailing how the franchise, and more specifically, Star Trek: Voyager, had an impact on her life, and it is lovely to see such an iconic actor and character being showcased during this celebratory time.

Star Trek Timelines retails at $60, so it is quite the investment, but readers will discover a recap of Star Trek's universe, including the various television shows which have aired over the years, as well as all the other media it has popped up in. Not only that, but the book aims to share information on the Star Trek universe as a whole; all the way from the Big Bang that created the universe to the many significant moments that have made the fictional universe as successful as it is. As such, it will feature some of the most beloved entries, such as The Original Series, The Next Generation, Deep Space Nine, Voyager, and Enterprise, as well as more recent television shows like Discovery, Strange New Worlds, and Starfleet Academy.

With the Star Trek universe being set, well, across the universe, Star Trek Timelines has a lot to cover, but you will be pleased to hear that it will also delve into various alternate timelines, such as the iconic Mirror Universe, and even Voyager's unforgettable "Year of Hell" storyline that I am sure none of us have forgotten. With this being one of Captain Janeway's most memorable storylines, it was obvious that it needed to be included, especially with Mulgrew endorsing the book herself.

Star Trek Timelines: A Visual Voyage Through Generations of History is now available to purchase, and just in time for Christmas. So, if you have a Star Trek lover in your life, you may have just found the perfect gift to surprise them with.

#3355. Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

Continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a big enough challenge. Doing so on the small screen adds an extra element of difficulty. Incredibly, "Blade Runner 2099" has overcome the odds to deliver yet another intoxicating excursion into the techno-industrial urban decay-scape so magically realized back in 1982's "Blade Runner" and so faithfully recreated in 2017's "Blade Runner 2049." As such, the Blade Runner franchise is now surely the most consistent on-screen sci-fi saga ever made. (Setting aside sci-fi sagas that are directed by the same person the whole time, like James Cameron's "Avatar.")

It's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget. Yet director Ridley Scott and his production team managed to create one of the most believable and immersive worlds in cinema history. The famous "Hades" opening shot immediately plunges you into a future post-ecological collapse, in which technology seems to have almost grown on the wreckage of a fallen world like moss on fallen trees. The debris of society is adorned with neon and machinery, creating an environment in which past and future collide. "Blade Runner" might have been buried at the box office by "E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial," but it was an absolutely enthralling sci-fi adventure that came to define the genre.

As such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in new directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle. The "Dune" director's take on the world first introduced to audiences in 1982 was immediately familiar as the same one in which Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard did battle with Rutger Hauer's Roy Batty and his band of rogue Replicants. Yet it also felt appropriately evolved for the three-decade time jump. Surely "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't pull off the same trick — especially across eight episodes? Well, it has.

/Film's Bill Bria has hailed "Blade Runner 2099" as the best sci-fi show in years, and it's hard to disagree based solely on the production design. From the moment the show begins, we're immersed in the same world to which Ridley Scott introduced us back in 1982. In fact, "2099" recreates the "Hades" sequence so faithfully you'd think you were watching the original. It's a clever move, too. As the camera slow-zooms on the Tyrell Corporation building and evokes the tone and feel of Scott's film, it establishes "2099" as very much belonging to the "Blade Runner" legacy. But we soon discover that this is not Rick Deckard's future.

80 years after Harrison Ford's Blade Runner absconded with Rachael (Sean Young), Replicants have now overthrown their human masters to become the dominant race. It's a major change that refreshes the franchise and helps make it more relevant than it's ever been at a time when the looming AI garbage future has prompted widespread talk of machines taking our jobs.

As such, it's more important than ever to maintain a tone and design language that's consistent with what came before, so as to reassure fans of the saga that this isn't some sort of wholesale reinvention of the franchise they love, but an evolution that plays out in the same world. "Blade Runner 2099" impressively pulls that off with its opening scene, and it only gets better from there.

When it comes to the world of "Blade Runner," fans know the deal: Retro futurism and cyberpunk aesthetics meet noirish expressionism in a technological nightmare future. Many franchises have tried to emulate the aesthetic to varying degrees of success, but there is only one "Blade Runner." As Christopher Nolan once told the Directors Guild of America while discussing Ridley Scott's film, it conjures "that feeling that there was this whole world outside the frame of the scene. You really felt there were things going on outside of those rooms where you've seen the film take place."

"Blade Runner 2099" has somehow managed to make every one of its scenes feel like they belong in that same world. With that in mind, it's truly remarkable how consistent the Blade Runner universe has remained across almost a half-century's worth of projects, each of which has been separated by many years. Even the best sci-fi franchises struggle to pull off what is, admittedly, an almost impossible trick.

The "Terminator" movies have never been able to recapture the intoxicating, doom-laden sci-fi slasher tone that made the first two films so memorable. The "Alien" franchise, meanwhile, has made a point of switching up its style and tone with each successive film — though more recent projects have tried to evoke the feeling of the 1979 original. "Blade Runner" films, however, all feel part of a cohesive whole that gives the entire saga this uncanny sense of existing in a real alternate timeline somewhere — as if we're witnessing an epic, decades-spanning dream play out in the mind of a dying Replicant. Regardless of how you feel about "2099" as a whole, its visual and tonal achievements simply can't be denied.

"Blade Runner 2099" Season 1 is now streaming on Prime Video.

#3353. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen? Watch ‘The Sheep Detectives’ VFX Supervisor Break Down the ‘Sheep-Isms’ That Made His Characters Stand Out

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#3352. 10 Classic Books Worth Reading Over and Over

Timeless stories that reveal something new with every reread

Most of us treat classic literature like a checklist to conquer in high school or college and then never touch those books again. You power through the plot, underline a few quotes for a term paper, and move on to whatever else is new. The catch is that great books rarely reveal their most fascinating tricks on the first pass. When you already know the ending, your brain stops racing for answers and begins to notice the machinery holding all those mysteries and themes together. Suddenly, an unreliable narrator's sleight of hand becomes obvious, or a throwaway line in chapter two hits like a freight train in light of later developments.

When you reread classic literature, everything changes: you stop rushing toward the finale and focus instead on how the author pulled it all off. Whether they reshape your perspective as you age or hide their best clues in plain sight, these 10 books reward you on every return trip.

Following an impoverished former student who believes extraordinary individuals can commit terrible acts in service of a greater purpose, Fyodor Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment is a descent into the mind of a murderer slowly unraveling under the weight of his own conscience. At the story’s center is Rodion Raskolnikov, a desperate and isolated young man living in the squalid slums of St. Petersburg who sets out to prove his own moral superiority. After murdering a pawnbroker, he is consumed by paranoia and the unbearable weight of his own guilt.​​​​​​​

Dostoevsky borrows the mechanics of a detective novel as he weaves Raskolnikov’s psychological fallout into the overriding mystery, setting aside the familiar detective-versus-killer plot to peer into the killer’s mind​​​​​​​. When you aren't racing through its pages to see whether Raskolnikov gets caught by the investigator Porfiry Petrovich, you savor the cat-and-mouse mind games between them. Every feverish rationalization and defensive outburst reads like a man slowly building his own prison cell.

Franz Kafka's The Trial is one of those rare books that becomes more unsettling the older you get. Josef K. is a bank employee who is suddenly arrested by an inexplicable authority for a crime that is never identified, though he is not confined to a conventional prison. Instead, Josef has to navigate a secretive court system whose offices occupy cramped attics in a residential neighborhood while trying to defend himself against charges nobody will explain.​​​​​​​ He appears before an unruly crowd of onlookers at a hearing and consults a bedridden lawyer named Herr Huld, who never seems to make any progress on his case.​​​​​​​

Kafka's masterpiece is a nightmare about institutional powerlessness, highlighting the absurdity of bureaucracy. It’s a compelling read​​​​​​​, a piece of fiction that proves the systems governing our lives can be profoundly irrational​​​​​​​. Its themes have only become more relevant with time, rewarding a second read once you stop looking for a logical explanation to the plot and start noticing Josef as he slowly pieces together the irrational system at play.

Few narrators divide readers quite like Holden Caulfield, a grieving teenager wandering through Manhattan in a red hunting hat after getting kicked out of yet another prep school. Across three wandering days in The Catcher in the Rye, J.D. Salinger lets Holden complain endlessly about the “phoniness” around him while quietly exposing the trauma and loneliness driving his cynicism.

Reading the novel in high school usually feels like an act of rebellion, as readers side with a misunderstood kid​​​​​​​, but coming back to it as an adult transforms the entire experience. Holden's defensive anger turns into a heartbreaking portrait of a boy terrified of growing up in the wake of losing his younger brother. Even the adults in the story land differently on a second pass, shifting from out-of-touch villains to exhausted people​​​​​​​ trying to keep a spiraling teenager from falling off a cliff.

Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness turns a riverboat expedition into a suffocating descent into human cruelty. The novella follows Charles Marlow, a British sailor hired to pilot a steamer up the Congo River to retrieve Kurtz, a highly successful ivory trader who has cut off contact and turned a remote outpost into his personal kingdom.

As Marlow pushes deeper into the stark jungle, the supposed civility of his European employers slowly gives way, revealing​​​​​​​ unchecked greed and violence. On first pass, it’s easy to get swept up in the atmospheric writing and mystery surrounding Kurtz, which is why rereading it feels like stepping into a completely different story. Knowing how the journey ends makes every return trip that much more fascinating, turning Conrad's fog-choked prose into a trail of clues about Marlow's own complicity.

There are plenty of novels that explore the pursuit of the American Dream, but few understand its inherent contradictions quite like F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby. Set during the Roaring Twenties, the plot mostly centers on Jay Gatsby, the mysterious and wealthy neighbor of Nick Carraway, the story’s narrator. Gatsby’s lavish parties conceal an obsessive desire to reunite with his former love, Daisy Buchanan, but hiding beneath all the champagne, extravagant cars, and glittering excess is a deeply tragic story about the impossibility of recapturing the past.

Fitzgerald's writing is top-notch, while the characters remain endlessly fascinating. It’s no surprise The Great Gatsby has remained recommended reading for years, offering a sharp critique of the American Dream whose subtle clues hit much harder once you already know how Gatsby's story ends​​​​​​​.

The Sun Also Rises is Ernest Hemingway's portrait of a generation struggling to find meaning in the aftermath of World War I. The protagonist, Jake Barnes, is an American journalist part of a circle of expatriate friends​​​​​​​ who drift through Paris and Spain in a haze of heavy drinking and late-night parties as they attempt to escape hidden emotional wounds.

At the center of the story is Jake's complicated relationship with Lady Brett Ashley, a woman he loves but cannot fully be with because of a war injury that has left him impotent. Hemingway's famously restrained prose gives the book much of its power on a second read, letting you catch the quiet heartbreak and disillusionment buried beneath seemingly ordinary conversations, a hallmark of Hemingway’s craft​​​​​​​.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice is one of the most enduring romantic novels ever written, and there's a reason readers keep returning to it more than two centuries after its publication. Set in rural Regency-era England, the story follows a sharp-witted young woman named Elizabeth Bennet navigating the expectations of English society while attempting to find a suitable marriage without sacrificing her independence. Her complicated relationship with the wealthy and aloof Mr. Darcy provides the foundation for an entertaining social satire that skewers class obsession and the assumptions we make about other people.

Much like The Sun Also Rises, the dialogue in Pride and Prejudice is razor-sharp, while Austen’s characters are wonderfully realized. Her observations about human behavior prove remarkably timeless, with every reread revealing how subtly she signals Darcy's early affection despite his stiff manners​​​​​​​. It's a delightful book that never seems to lose its charm, and only gets better the more times you experience Elizabeth's stubbornness.

A Tale of Two Cities is an enormous historical drama set against the backdrop of the French Revolution, following characters caught between the political upheaval of Paris and the relative stability of London. At its center is Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat attempting to escape his family's violent legacy, and Sydney Carton, a disillusioned English lawyer whose love for Darnay's wife, Lucie, places him​​​​​​​ on a path toward an extraordinary act of sacrifice.

Charles Dickens brings the chaos and brutality of revolutionary France to life while weaving together a deeply moving story about the possibility of personal transformation. It's a sweeping, emotionally powerful novel that builds toward one of literature's most unforgettable conclusions. Knowing the finale changes how every preceding chapter reads​​​​​​​, making Sydney Carton's early apathy and reckless drinking feel like quiet clues to the man he would inevitably become​​​​​​​.

Set in ancient India, Siddhartha tracks a young man who abandons his privileged upbringing to pursue spiritual enlightenment. Along the way, he tests himself through asceticism, material wealth, and romantic love, while seeking guidance from seasoned teachers​​​​​​​, gradually discovering that no outside philosophy can provide him with the answers he seeks​​​​​​​.

What makes Siddhartha so unforgettable on a reread is how it frames personal growth as something messy rather than linear. Real change often requires stumbling into failure or temptation first, forcing you to deal with immediate consequences before you can recognize what actually matters. It is a brisk read built for repeated visits, yet its lessons hold up across a lifetime.

On the surface, Jonas lives in a peaceful utopia where hunger, suffering, and social conflict have largely been eradicated, yet that stability depends on stripping away emotional depth, collective memory, and individual choice. At the Ceremony of Twelve in Lois Lowry's The Giver, Jonas is chosen as the next Receiver of Memory rather than receiving a standard community assignment​​​​​​​. His training with the old Receiver introduces him to sensations the rest of the community never experiences, from sled rides in deep snow to the warmth of sunshine and the shock of physical agony.

As Jonas absorbs such memories, he begins seeing cracks in his orderly world, especially as he notices flashes of color and questions​​​​​​​ the community's treatment of Gabriel, a young child who has been marked for release. Rereading The Giver makes the quiet dread much sharper because you already know what "release" actually means long before Jonas pieces it together. The polite rituals of the “evening telling of feelings” and the community’s calm routines seem less like signs of peace than evidence of a society sedated into forgetting what it gave up.​​​​​​​ Lowry trusts younger readers with heavy moral questions without ever talking down to them. Returning to the book years later hits differently because the horror shifts away from the shocking twists toward the quiet complicity of the adults who willingly traded away their humanity just to feel safe.

#3351. The Cliff Booth Movie Brings Back Two Key Characters From Once Upon A Time In Hollywood

This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth."

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher. But still, you had to wonder if any other familiar faces would pop up in this new mis-adventure.

Part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history. Thanks to the actions of Cliff, actress Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie) is not murdered by the Manson family. How does the entertainment world and Los Angeles change by 1977, when "Cliff Booth" takes place, because of that ripple effect? Tarantino wrote the script for "Cliff Booth," and if any filmmaker is equipped to dig into the nitty-gritty of such a change in Hollywood history, down to the most obscure B-pictures and forgotten TV, it's him.

Now, the major supporting cast of "Cliff Booth" is totally different. Cliff's best friend, actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) — for whom Cliff worked as a stunt double and driver back in 1969 — does not appear due to DiCaprio declining a cameo appearance. The movie mentions a few times that Rick moved to Australia and is currently starring in a popular TV show there, "Dingo Dan." Tarantino has also devised some stories about what happened to Rick after that fateful August 9, 1969 night.

But a few of the fictionalized Hollywood characters return for brief cameos: Margot Robbie as Sharon Tate, Timothy Olyphant as actor James Stacy, and even Nicholas Hammond as TV director Sam Wanamaker (in a smaller role).

One of the Quentin Tarantino Easter eggs in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes, a fictional brand that appears in other Tarantino movies. The actress in the commercial is Sharon Tate, with Cliff smiling at her and likely recalling how he saved her life. "Once Upon A Time In Hollywood" cast Sharon Tate in an angelic light, down to giving her the happy ending that reality didn't. But revisiting her in greater depth, like what became of her marriage to Roman Polanski or how her acting career played out, would risk adding a dash of salt to that sweet ending.

The alternate history of Sharon Tate in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" earned obvious comparisons to Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," which also starred Brad Pitt (as Lieutenant Aldo Raine, leader of the Nazi-killing Basterds). In that movie, Adolf Hitler (Martin Wutke) dies at the hands of Jewish soldiers instead of by suicide. That leads into Timothy Olyphant's "Cliff Booth" cameo, which feels self-recursively inspired by "Basterds."

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" mixes real Hollywood history with pastiche. Much of the first half sees Dalton filming a guest spot on a TV Western, "Lancer," which was a real show back in the late '60s. Olyphant appears as the real-life star of "Lancer," James Stacy, and the episode is directed by Nicholas Hammond's Sam Wanamaker, the real director of the "Lancer" pilot episode. "Cliff Booth" gives us another glimpse of Stacy and Wanamaker working in this alternate timeline's television industry.

Since 1969, Cliff Booth has become a fixer: someone who (violently) solves problems for Hollywood fixtures wrapped up with criminals. Fictional TV star Charlie Winters (Scott Caan) becomes one of his clients. The movie includes a newsreel style montage, narrated by Quentin Tarantino himself, recounting Winters' rise to TV stardom.

One of Winters' shows is "Enemy Territory," about a U.S. pilot trapped behind enemy lines in Europe during World War 2. The narrator describes the show as "'The Fugitive' with Nazis, but 'The Fugitive' with Nazis is a fun idea." (I'd watch it!) We see Winters shooting a scene where his character threatens a Gestapo officer into helping him rescue a captured American general. The officer is played by none other than Timothy-Olyphant-as-James-Stacy, doing a broad German accent with a high pitch reminiscent of Christoph Waltz's Colonel Hans Landa from "Inglourious Basterds."

Sam Wanamaker is directing the scene. Stacy's performance is being criticized as "a smidge cavalier" — so Winters puts a live round in the prop gun with which his character is threatening the Gestapo officer. Stacy, sure enough, begins acting like a man whose life is being balanced on the edge of a trigger.

Casting Olyphant as James Stacy was a nod to how his real most famous roles are on Western TV shows — namely, Sheriff Seth Bullock in HBO's "Deadwood" and Deputy U.S. Marshal Raylan Givens in the Kentucky-set neo-Western "Justified." But Olyphant has got range beyond playing cowboys, and his comic energy in his "Cliff Booth" cameo is just more evidence of that.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is playing in theaters, with a Netflix release date of December 23, 2026.

#3350. Netflix’s 6-Part Political Conspiracy Thriller Delivers A Masterclass In Psychological Suspense

Netflix's 6-part political conspiracy thriller delivers a masterclass in psychological suspense, with gripping twists, dangerous secrets, and deep themes of betrayal. Starring Richard Madden of Game of Thrones fame, this Netflix limited series is one of the easiest shows on the platform to start and finish in just one weekend, sporting a total runtime of roughly 6 hours and 7 minutes across six masterfully crafted episodes. The series is a phenomenal showcase of building tension from its very first episode, led by a morally conflicted protagonist.

Bodyguard remains one of Netflix's best political thriller miniseries of all time, delivering relentless psychological suspense across a tight 6-part story that is full of well-executed plot twists. The 2-time Emmy-nominated series earned a 93% Rotten Tomatoes score and is still an elite quick binge option 8 years after its premiere, featuring outstanding performances, dazzling action sequences, and fantastic character development. Bodyguard follows a war veteran and police officer named David Budd (Madden) who is assigned to protect a controversial yet high-ranking government official he disagrees with politically.

Bodyguard begins with a compelling high-stakes situation, forcing David to respond to a potentially catastrophic situation after he suspects a suicide bomber on a train heading for London. Aboard the train with his children, David must rely on his quick thinking and his advanced training methods to neutralize the threat, all while protecting his family at the same time. All this happens within the first 20 or so minutes of Bodyguard, setting up the rest of the unfolding action that includes even more threats of violence against the politician David is assigned to protect, Julia Montague, played by Keeley Hawes.

Before David and Julia ever meet in the series, Julia already has a target on her back for signing a new bill into law that increases the government's ability to monitor digital communications between citizens, which is met with public outrage. This establishes the narrative engine that sustains the tension built within the first episode throughout the 6-part series, with the threat of retaliation and violence present at any given moment. Beyond the physical threats, David is diagnosed with PTSD, which greatly influences his behavior and ability to make decisions. This, along with his differing political views from Julia, creates psychological suspense beneath the surface-level violence.

David's complicated psychological profile and complex history with trauma make him a fascinating protagonist in Bodyguard, as he can often be quite unpredictable for someone who is entrusted to protect the life of a high-ranking political figure. That said, plot developments after the first few episodes of Bodyguard would be confusing for any character, as larger conspiracies begin to reveal themselves and it becomes increasingly difficult for David to determine who he can trust. Because of these unique psychological elements, Bodyguard elevates itself beyond a standard political conspiracy thriller on Netflix, allowing it to exist in an elite category of its own.

Netflix's new 4-part crime thriller is trending #2 worldwide, offering a gripping one-night binge inspired by a disturbing real-life murder case.

Madden delivers one of his career best roles as David Budd, bringing all the complexities of the David Budd character to life in convincing and compelling ways. Most critics highlight Madden's performance as the greatest part of the 6-part Netflix series and one of the key reasons why it's so binge-worthy from start to finish. Variety writes of Bodyguard, "Both juicy in its delving into character psychology and rippingly ready to tear up its playbook as it goes, it's a six-episode ride that demands, and rewards, a quick binge."

Netflix has a great new slate of streaming releases that are worth checking out this holiday weekend, including Black Doves season 2, The Hunting Wives season 2, and The Trials of Karen Read. However, if you're looking for a phenomenally suspenseful show that's guaranteed not to disappoint, Bodyguard is about as good as it gets as far as 6-part political thrillers go on Netflix.

#3349. The Best Gifts for Every Tech Nerd in Your Life

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

Our grandparents could drop some treats in a sock and call it Christmas, secure in the knowledge that their children would be delighted by an orange. These days, though, everyone from your tech-obsessed granny to your cutting-edge teen wants to be impressed. Luckily, there's a mind-blowing high-tech gadget out there for everyone.

I don't know anyone who wouldn't appreciate finding these display glasses in their Christmas stocking. The Xbx a01s are sunglasses you can plug into any device with a USB-C port to create your own personal, private monitor. The resulting picture is the equivalent of a 142" TV. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz, and the glasses support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling and billions of colors, all in a package that weighs only 62 grams. In other words: It's an HD TV you can carry in your pocket and wear on your face. The $299 list price won't break your wallet either. They're the best smart glasses for most people. Check out my full review for more details.

It can be hard to buy a gift for a health-focused person. They usually don't want booze and they like putting in effort. But the Whoop Peak 5 fitness tracker will brighten the Christmas morning of the most diehard athlete. It's more versatile than a watch (you can wear it on your bicep and even in your underwear) and it monitors heart rate, respiratory rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen levels, daily activity, and sleep—basically everything I don't worry about. Check out Lifehacker's senior health editor Beth Skwarecki's in-depth look at the Whoop Peak 5 for more details.

You cannot go wrong with a GoPro. The company's easy-to-use, hard-to-break cameras are synonymous with "action photography" and compact enough to fit in a stocking. If there's a snowboarder, skateboarder, kayaker, or BMX racer on your list, this is a must. Even if your giftee isn't an adventurer, the GoPro Hero 13 supports additional lenses and filters that let users go beyond the "gnarly fish-eye, dude" photography and videography of past generations. Check out associate tech editor Michelle Ehrhardt's GoPro Hero 13 review for more details.

Everyone wants their own droid. Beni from Mondo Robotics is a camera robot that takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control Beni with the remote, or simply tell it to follow you. It can be set to track you from behind, from the side, or it can circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote on the fly, so there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's freakin' adorable. The $799 list price might be a bit steep for most gift-givers, but as far as how well it works and how much fun I've had using it, it's worth the money.

The R36 Max 2 retro handheld game console lets you take your gaming anywhere. It comes with over 20,000 games pre-installed, so you can play every title from classic consoles like the Atari 2600 or the PlayStation 1, as well as just about every arcade game anyone ever dropped a coin into, all for less than $100. I paid more than that in quarters just to beat Dragon's Lair!

I'm obsessed with the Yamaha Seqtrak. It crams a drum machine, sequencer, sampler, three separate synthesizers, and a speaker into a package small enough to put into a Christmas stocking. It's a complete mobile studio—everything you need to produce a song or beat—but it also integrates with your computer's DAW and other MIDI gear to become part of your home studio. All that for only $300!

The Flipper Zero is a must-have device for the hardcore, glasses-wearing, circuit-bender type of techie. Its ability to do evil deeds like hack ATMs is greatly exaggerated, but the Flipper is still a technological Swiss Army knife that lets you read and manipulate the invisible waves around you, from radio waves to RFID, NFC, Bluetooth, and wifi signals. It's educational, fascinating, and powerful; how you use that power is your business.

If you're giving a gift to a would-be Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, this miniature, wireless microscope will rock their holiday. It's easy to set up, works with PCs, Android, or iOS devices, magnifies things up to 1000x, and takes 1080p pictures of your discoveries.

#3348. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026? ‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

#3347. 10 Hacks Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are important. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

If you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

Using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having said that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

Haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an issue where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a big problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That said, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift issues in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area quickly.

If you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same issues, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently shows a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.
