#3319. 7 Agatha Christie Books Inspired by Real Crimes

Beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature.   Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026.  Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is currently in the process of writing.

Agatha Christie did not write true crime. Instead, her talent was imagining complex and compelling puzzles surrounding a murder. Several of them were inspired by experiences from her own life, such as working as a nurse during WWI or traveling through the Middle East, accompanying her archeologist second husband to excavation sites. But not even the Queen of Crime could avoid the coverage of real crimes in newspapers and media. Although the stories and characters are always her own, some of Christie's most famous murder mysteries take inspiration from real-life cases.

Many real crimes and criminals are explicitly mentioned in Agatha Christie's novels and short stories. "Remember the long-continued successes of Jack the Ripper," Hercule Poirot tells Captain Arthur Hastings in the 1936 novel The ABC Murders. It is often believed the story of the Victorian serial killer inspired the plot of the book. Christie also held a deep fascination for the 1892 Lizzie Borden case, and the rhyme inspired by it is recited in After the Funeral. Other times, Christie did more than just borrow the general idea of a crime, and incorporated specific details related to a murder for her stories. Here are some of the most fascinating cases.

In 1916, during World War I, Agatha Christie was working in a hospital dispensary and was bored. Christie decided to use this time to write a detective novel. "Since I was surrounded by poisons, perhaps it was natural that death by poisoning should be the method I selected," Christie herself wrote in her autobiography. Inspired by the detective book tradition, she created her own iconic investigator. He would be Belgian, like many of the refugees she was interacting with. His name would be Hercule Poirot.

The Mysterious Affair at Styles was inspired by not one but two real murder cases. The fictional death of wealthy Emily Inglethorp at her Essex country house, Styles Court, has many parallels to that of Frances Garnett Orme. The 49-year-old spiritualist was found dead from poison in her locked room in the Savoy Hotel in Mussoorie, India, in 1911. Orme's companion was the main suspect. The book also echoes the story of William Palmer, an English doctor convicted in 1856 of poisoning his friend, John Cook, with strychnine, the same poison Agatha Christie uses in the book. It was suspected that Palmer had also killed several members of his family, including four of his children. In addition to the murder method, Agatha Christie's novel also includes several key details from the Palmer case, such as coffee left in a hallway, an inquest at the village inn and a pharmacist who sold the poison thinking it would be used to kill a dog.

Billie Carleton was a British musical comedy actress in WWI London. By 18, she was a star. Four years later, and days after the end of the war, Carleton was found dead of an apparent drug overdose. The night before, she had attended the Victory Ball at the Royal Albert Hall dressed in a scandalous semi-transparent dress designed by her friend Reggie de Veulle. An investigation found De Veulle had provided Carleton with the substances and revealed he had been part of a secret underground London cocaine trafficking ring. He was sentenced to eight months in prison.

Agatha Christie's The Affair at the Victory Ball, one of the first Hercule Poirot short stories, takes readers to the inside of British high society. It is set during this luxurious celebration of the end of the war, which a group of people attended dressed in the costumes of the Italian commedia dell’arte. During the ball, Lord Cronshaw, dressed as Harlequin, is stabbed to death. The morning after the ball, his fiancée, actress Coco Courtnay, is found dead in her bed from a cocaine overdose. Christie never said the story was based on Billie Carleton’s death, but the details speak for themselves.

On the evening of 31 January 1910, Cora Crippen, an extravagant music hall singer, disappeared from her London home. Her husband, the quiet American homeopath Hawley Harvey Crippen, claimed she had left him and moved to the U.S. Soon after, his mistress, Ethel Le Neve, moved into his house and began wearing Mrs Crippen's clothes and jewelry. When the case caught the police's attention, Dr. Crippen and Le Neve fled on a ship to Canada, with Le Neve disguised as a boy. However, the ship's captain recognized the pair and notified his superiors using wireless telegraphy. It was the first time this technology was used to track a criminal. In their absence, the police had searched the home and found human remains. Police officers then jumped onto a faster ship and chased the doctor and his mistress. They were arrested, and Dr. Crippen was found guilty of the murder. Le Neve was acquitted and later changed her name to distance herself from the case.

The story of the Crippen murder made international headlines, and even caught Agatha Christie's eye. She borrowed many details from the crime for her witty novel Mrs. McGinty's Dead, in which James Bentley is convicted of killing the elderly Mrs. McGinty. Hercule Poirot is asked to take on the case. The trail leads him to a newspaper clipping Mrs. McGinty kept that profiles women connected to notorious murder cases. One of them is Eva Kane, the mistress in the fictional "Craig case". Like Le Neve, Kane was found not guilty of the murder of her lover's wife. In the book, Kane changes her name and leaves the country. Her story is the key to the case.

The Mousetrap still holds the record for the longest-running play in the world. The production, which first opened in 1952, is the same that can be seen today in London's West End. It is based on a radio play written by Agatha Christie as a birthday present for Queen Mary, titled Three Blind Mice. Christie then expanded the plot into a short story, but she requested that it not be published until the play had closed. Since The Mousetrap is still running, this has not happened yet in the UK, although the story has been published in the U.S.

Both The Mousetrap and Three Blind Mice are based on the same case, the tragic death of 12-year-old Dennis O'Neill in 1945. Little Dennis and his younger brother, Terence (Terry) O'Neill, aged 9, were placed in foster care and sent to live with Reginald and Esther Gough on a remote English farm. Under their care, the children were beaten and barely fed. Less than a year later, Dennis died after being struck on the chest and beaten. The couple was charged with manslaughter and neglect in a grueling case made worse when young Terry was asked to act as a witness in the couple's trial. Terry's testimony angered the whole country and helped bring about the Children Act of 1948. The case became a clear inspiration for Agatha Christie's story, in which three fictional foster care children are sent to live in Longridge Farm, where one of them dies. Years later, one of their siblings takes revenge.

Toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a new Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

People tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

You have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

You are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

The second Poirot story Agatha Christie wrote takes the detective to France. When he and Captain Hastings arrive, they are met with the news that the man they came to see, Paul Renauld, has died. His widow, Eloise Renauld, claims a group of masked men broke into her villa in the middle of the night, tied her up to the bed, and dragged her husband to the golf course, where they stabbed him to death. The investigation takes a turn when a second body is discovered, killed in a nearly identical way.

The setup of Murder on the Links follows that of one of France's most notorious murder trials. In May 1908, Marguerite Steinheil was found gagged and bound to a bed. Like Mrs. Renauld, Marguerite claimed she was attacked by intruders who killed her mother and husband, the painter Adolphe Steinheil. Marguerite was already infamous in Paris. Years before, she had been the mistress of French President Félix Faure, who had died in her arms after suffering a stroke. Marguerite tried to frame several people for the murder of her family members, but she was found out. It was widely believed that she herself had staged the intrusion to murder her husband. With no proof to back the accusation, a French jury acquitted Marguerite Stenheil in 1909 after an extremely sensationalistic trial.

Just as with a good murder-mystery, a list can take a turn. In this case, it is worth highlighting The Pale Horse as the only Agatha Christie book that inspired a crime, helped solve another, and saved several lives. In the novel, Mrs Davis gives her last confession to Father Gorman along with a list of names. Shortly after, the priest is murdered, and the people on the list begin dying from what seem to be natural causes.

At the heart of this book is a poison. It is made from an odorless heavy metal called thallium, which, if ingested in small doses, can cause symptoms such as hair loss and gastrointestinal distress that doctors routinely misdiagnose. The poison is said to have inspired Graham Young, known as "The Teacup Poisoner". In 1972, Young was accused of lacing his coworkers' tea and coffee with thallium and antimony, killing two colleagues. Some accounts say Young was caught thanks to a doctor who had read Agatha Christie's novel and became suspicious. Thallium was also the method used by George Trepal to poison his neighbors, the Carr family, killing Peggy Carr. An undercover detective who had been in Trepal's home recalled seeing a copy of The Pale Horse.

Agatha Christie's book also saved lives. In 1975, more than a decade after the novel was published, Christie received a letter from a reader in South America who had noticed a friend suffering from unexplained hair loss and pain. The reader remembered the plot of The Pale Horse and alerted the woman's physicians, who confirmed she had suffered thallium poisoning. Two years later, a one-year-old Qatari girl was flown to London. She was in a coma caused by an illness no doctors could diagnose. It was Marsha Maitland, a nurse in the hospital who had been reading The Pale Horse, who suggested thallium poisoning. The test came back positive, allowing doctors to find the treatment that saved the toddler's life.

One child was kidnapped. Six people died as a direct consequence. This is the tragic arc at the heart of what is perhaps Agatha Christie's most famous novel, Murder on the Orient Express. In the book, Hercule Poirot is tasked with investigating the murder of American businessman Samuel Ratchett aboard the luxurious Orient Express. All the suspects in the murder are staying inside the same train, trapped in Yugoslavia in the middle of a snowstorm. Poirot soon finds that the murder is connected to an older tragedy: the kidnapping and murder of little Daisy Armstrong. The conclusion to the story is what makes it so compelling. It is tragic and simply brilliant.

In the book, Agatha Christie aims to give a sense of justice to a real-life tragic crime. In 1932, 20-month-old Charles Lindbergh Jr, was taken from his crib in his New Jersey home. He was the son of the most famous aviator in the world, whose name he shared. The authors of the crime requested a $50,000 ransom. The parents paid. Soon after, the baby's body was found in the woods near the house. Weeks later, a young maid, Violet Sharpe, killed herself after being questioned by the police as a suspect. The crime was so famous it led to the passing of the Federal Kidnapping Act (the "Little Lindbergh Law"). Agatha Christie's fictional Armstrong case reproduces the Lindbergh case almost point for point. Except, of course, real crimes are rarely clear-cut. In 1934, a carpenter named Bruno Richard Hauptmann was arrested for the crime. Hauptmann was executed in 1936, although his guilt continues to be called into question even today.

#3315. iOS 27 lets you use two iPhones with the same phone number

9to5Mac is brought to you by Tello Mobile. Switching to Tello Mobile can bring the cost of your plan down to as little as $5 a month, or an unlimited plan for just $25 a month, all on America’s largest 5G network. See all of the available plans at tello.com.

Among iOS 27’s many new features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads. Signal's end-to-end encryption keeps prying eyes out, but if you use agentic AI on your device, your chats may not be as locked down as you think.

Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11. While Signal cannot guarantee that AI won't have access to your data, there are a few protections now available for those on iOS and Android as well.

The main workaround in Signal for now is to restrict screenshots and screen recordings inside the app, though this does not prevent AI agents from potentially grabbing content from other parts of your device. According to Signal's support documents, these protections will now be enabled by default on iOS 27 and Android with the latest versions of the Signal app.

#3313. YNW Melly Wants Technology Search Thrown Out, Judge Approves

YNW Melly's trying a ton of different legal tactics to win his upcoming murder trial ... including getting evidence obtained from an iPhone thrown out -- and the judge signed off on his request.

Here's the deal ... last month, YNW Melly filed legal documents arguing that data obtained from his Instagram, Snapchat, Google and iPhone obtained by investigators back in 2024 should be disregarded -- claiming the search warrant obtained was overbroad and no probable cause established in the affidavit could justify the search and seizure.

His side also alleged that a detective accessed requested material illegally ... claiming the judge in Melly's first trial even raked the guy over the coals for not acting "in good faith" when he "conducted an illegal search" of the data.

Prosecutors fired back, arguing investigators didn't do anything wrong by legally obtaining previously suppressed evidence after securing another warrant for that evidence.

Ultimately, the judge sided with Melly ... ruling they can't use the evidence at trial.

As you know ... Melly is accused of killing YNW Sakchaser and YNW Juvy back in 2018. YNW secured a mistrial in 2023 ... though he's remained locked up in the years since, awaiting his retrial.

#3311. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 1 Recap: What To Remember Before Netflix’s Steamy Thriller Returns

Netflix’s The Hunting Wives is one of the streamer's most addictive series: a soapy, raunchy romp that is delightfully unhinged from start to finish. Grounded in the sizzling chemistry between stars Malin Akerman and Brittany Snow, the show is steamy, sexy, and wildly entertaining, the sort of unashamed guilty pleasure TV that was made for the “just one more episode” binge model.

Based on the novel of the same name by bestselling author May Cobb, the series exploded in popularity following its debut last summer, racking up streaming minutes and TikTok edits while thrilling viewers with its nonstop plot twists. The story revolves around a group of wealthy Texas housewives who sport designer fashions and are all heavily armed. They’re at the center of everything in their small conservative town of Maple Brook, Texas, whether it's passing judgment from the pews at church, throwing back margaritas at a local honky tonk, or having ill-advised affairs.

These women are messy with a capital M, and that’s before they find themselves at the center of a murder investigation. Here's a quick recap of everything you need to remember about The Hunting Wives’ twisty first season before Season 2 premieres.

The series follows Tesla-driving, East Coast liberal transplant Sophie O’Neill (Snow), who moves to Maple Brook with her family for a fresh start after a devastating personal trauma. Her husband Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) lands a job with Jed Banks (Dermot Mulroney), a wealthy oil businessman who is being courted to run for governor. Sophie hits it off immediately with his wife, Margo (Akerman), bonding over prescription drugs and anxiety in a fundraiser bathroom.

Drawn into the lavish world of the Texas elite, Sophie quickly learns that things are much more complicated (and salacious) than they initially appear. Margo’s essentially open marriage means that she’s not only sexually involved with her BFF Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), but she’s also secretly having an affair with her other BFF Jill’s (Katie Lowes) teenage son, Brad (George Ferrier). (Anything goes in Texas!) And when Brad’s high school girlfriend Abby (Madison Wolfe) turns up dead after a night of drinking and partying at Margo’s forest cabin — the same night Sophie’s gun goes missing — everyone’s a suspect, including Sophie herself.

Abby’s murder is the primary narrative drive of The Hunting Wives' first season, pushing Margo and Sophie closer together as they scramble to cover up their night of blackout-drunk escapades with a pair of high school boys. Along the way, the two ultimately give in to the attraction that’s been simmering between them since the series’ first episode and become intimate, not only sharing steamy hook-ups, but building a real emotional bond.

Unfortunately, all of that is shattered when Sophie realizes that Margo actually killed Abby. The teen found out that Margo not only had an affair with Brad, but had gotten pregnant and had an abortion. Abby's threats to expose Margo's secrets led to Margo shooting her with Sophie’s gun. Margo ultimately frames Brad’s mother, Jill, for the crime, leading to a standoff in the Thompson home that results in several other deaths, including Abby’s mother, Starr (Chrissy Metz), and Jill herself. (It is easier for the police to blame a dead woman, after all.)

In 1985 these four put their names on one record and called it Highwayman, and the title track went straight to number one on the country chart. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

Nothing gets to you and you have no plans to stop. Willie left Nashville for Texas, made a sparse concept album the label thought was unfinished, and it turned out to be the record that proved the whole outlaw idea worked.

You carry weight and people feel it when you walk in. Cash wore black on purpose, played prisons when nobody else would, and spent a career siding with whoever the room had decided to look down on.

Nobody tells you how to do your job. Waylon forced RCA to let him pick his own songs, his own band and his own producer, which simply was not done in Nashville, and every artist who came after him benefited from it.

You have had about four lives and you are not finished. Kristofferson was a Rhodes Scholar and an army helicopter pilot before he took a job sweeping floors at a Nashville studio so somebody might eventually read his songs.

Although Jill’s death — and the fact that the police now believe she's responsible for Abby's murder — results in Sophie being released from prison, it’s far from the end of her problems. Margo tells her volatile brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), who has a substance abuse problem and has frequent run-ins with the law, that her friend/ex/situationship knows the truth about what she did.

After a lifetime of playing the protective big brother, Kyle takes things into his own hands, running Sophie off a deserted road and trying to intimidate her. Terrified, Sophie runs Kyle over with her car before dragging his body to a nearby quarry to hide the evidence. In the season’s final moments, Sophie answers a call from Kyle’s phone — it’s Margo, asking if he “took care” of Sophie.

If The Hunting Wives’ first season is anything to go by, we can expect even bigger, wilder swings in Season 2. Both Margo and Sophie may technically still be free, but they also have literal bodies in their closets, and in a town as small as Maple Brook, it seems unlikely that those secrets will stay buried forever.

It’s also unlikely that the two women will stay at odds for too long. After all, their relationship is the emotional engine that propels the series, and things feel very unfinished between them. Sure, Sophie knows the truth about Abby Jackson’s death, but now that she’s a murderer herself, it’s basically impossible for her to go to the police. And while Margo’s currently in the dark about Kyle’s fate, even if/when she finds out, would she even be able to tell anyone, given Sophie’s knowledge of her own crimes? (We won’t talk about what’s going to happen when Margo realizes Kyle’s dead at her girlfriend’s hand, er, wheel...) But whatever happens, Season 2 is guaranteed to be a wild ride in more ways than one.

The Hunting Wives Season 2 premieres November 26 on Netflix.

#3310. Two Budget Smartwatches That Make Perfect Gifts

If you or someone on your shopping list wants a new smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from. The problem is, a lot of them can be quite pricey. Apple's cheapest smartwatch, the SE 3, starts at $249, and its other selections only skyrocket from there. On the flip side, the risk in picking a smartwatch that's too inexpensive is that the manufacturer likely made a series of sacrifices to get the price that low. At a certain point, the tradeoff just isn't worth it.

Luckily, you do have options. There are two smartwatches on the market that aren't just cheaper than the competition, they're not even in the same ballpark. And while you shouldn't expect the same capabilities as you would on flagship wearables, these devices are perfectly usable, both as fitness trackers and smartwatches—all while spending well below $100 a pop. CNET put both smartwatches through their paces to make these determinations, so you know whichever model you get, you won't be picking up a wearable paperweight.

Contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter. Amazfit is its own company, and produces a wide selection of smartwatch options. The Bip 6 happens to be the company's latest budget smartwatch, with an MSRP of just $79.99. In most cases, a price that low would be a red flag for a smartwatch, but not in the Bip 6's case.

The Amazfit Bip 6 holds its own against other flagship smartwatches. That's true on a surface level: This watch looks your average smartwatch, rather than a cheap imitation. In fact, at first glance, I'd bet most people would assume the Bip 6 is actually an Apple Watch. It has a rounded square design with a large 1.97-inch display with a resolution of 390 by 450 pixels (though there's no Always-On display). This isn't a cheap display, either: Amazfit put an AMOLED screen on the watch, which looks great indoors—though CNET Labs struggled to see the screen in direct sunlight.

Where the Bip 6 really shines, however, is with fitness tracking. This watch supports GPS, which makes tracking outdoor runs possible without a smartphone. CNET Labs found that it takes about 10 seconds to find a GPS signal, but once it connects, you're set. While running, the Bip 6 reliably tracks your heart rate. CNET Labs compared its sensor to the Polar chest strap HR monitor and found it on par, though, like other smartwatches, the Bip 6 is slower at detecting heart rate spikes. You'll get data like cadence and stride while tracking runs, and strength training and muscle groups while working out indoors. For example, CNET Labs found that it correctly identified arm muscle exercises while testing the watch during a pilates session.

You also get some health and wellness features, too. The Bip 6 can measure heart rate variations, body temperature changes, sleep stages, and even your breathing quality. Its One Tap Measuring mode supports a single reading for heart rate, SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation), stress, and breathing rate, and it supports cycle tracking—though CNET specifies it can't track skin temperature like other smartwatches and health trackers. There's an optional subscription that provides AI coaching tools and looks out for health conditions like sleep apnea and insomnia. While health and wellness tracking is solid, note that CNET Labs found Amazfit's app, Zepp, to be confusing, since it simply displays your data without much context or explanation.

For an $80 smartwatch, the Bip 6 has an excellent battery life. CNET Labs found that the watch could be pushed to its limits—multiple workouts using GPS, heart rate tracking, keeping the display on during workouts—and still run for eight days before needing a charge. In fact, reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana speculates you could push the Bip 6 to Amazfit's two-week battery life claim by limiting some of the most intensive settings and features. The only downside here is that there is no fast charging, so it will take about two hours to get back to 100%. But if you're only charging the watch once every week or two, that isn't much of a burden. There's also no charger in the box, so you'll need to use a separate USB-C cable.

As a smartwatch, the Bip 6 can be a mixed bag. CNET found that the UI was clunky and sluggish, and the OS requires some user intervention before it's as usable as a standard Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch. While the watch has a voice assistant, Flow, CNET found it to be borderline unusable. However, CNET says Android users can reply to texts with a keyboard or dictation without needing the assistant. iPhone users can't do the same by default, but by downloading a third-party app, they can jerry-rig the watch to send and receive texts.

Based on CNET Labs' testing, the Amazfit Bip 6 is one of the best budget smartwatches you can buy. For $80, you get a reliable workout tracker that looks like most standard watches on the market. And while you're making some sacrifices at this price point, they're largely worth it for $80.

While the Amazfit is a good choice for both iPhone and Android users, the Galaxy Fit 3 might be the best choice for Samsung users. This isn't an option for iPhone users, and while it works with all Android devices, you get some Samsung-specific perks if you have a Galaxy phone.

The Galaxy Fit 3 is even cheaper than the Amazfit Bip 6: This watch is only $60, which makes it among the cheapest smartwatches you can buy. Now, this doesn't look like your average smartwatch. Samsung opted for a fitness tracker-like design, with a long 1.6-inch (40mm) AMOLED display. But for a fitness tracker/smartwatch hybrid, it's a solid look.

In CNET's testing, one of the Galaxy Fit 3's biggest strengths is its battery life—though it pales in comparison to the Bip 6. When pushed to its limits, the Fit 3 can run three days in between charges, though Samsung claims you can get it up to 13 days with the right settings. While the Amazfit has it beat, the Fit 3 might sound like a dream compared to other smartwatches, even from Samsung. Unlike the Bip 6, the Fit 3 supports fast charging. You can fill the watch up completely in just over an hour.

CNET did find that the "smart" elements of this wearable were a bit lacking, however. The Fit 3 doesn't support voice dictation or mobile payments like other watches do, and unless you have a Galaxy phone, you won't be able to access the camera remote or sync your alarms. And while the Amazfit Bip 6's "Flow" is hardly reliable, the Fit 3 doesn't have an assistant at all. You can see incoming calls and decline (but not answer) them, and you can send prewritten responses to text messages, but not initiate them. Still, CNET found that Samsung added the essentials: You have an alarm, calculator, weather app, camera remote, and, of course, the Samsung Health app. (What kind of health tracker would this be without it?)

CNET found that the Fit 3 is a reliable fitness tracker, particularly for $60. You can track over 100 different workouts, and the watch automatically logs exercises like runs, walks, rowing, and elliptical sessions—if you enable auto-tracking, that is. It also supports swimming with its IP68 water resistance rating. CNET Labs found that the heart rate tracking was "generally accurate" when compared to the Polar chest strap, though its slower with registering heart rate spikes. Interestingly, the heart rate tracker was a bit delayed in testing, but once CNET reviewed the data in the health app, the data had corrected to be largely accurate. You also get high and low heart rate alerts, though no ECG app. (The $249 Apple Watch SE 3 also omits this feature.)

In CNET's testing, the sleep tracker on the Fit 3 was useful, if not entirely accurate. The watch can detect your sleep stages and look out for snoring using your Galaxy phone's mic. Like other health trackers, you get a sleep score, but CNET found it a bit inaccurate, since it rated a six and a half hour sleep session "Excellent" (91/100).

Still, the Fit 3 is really the only other smartwatch option at this price point that people should seriously consider. Until another company drops a product around this MSRP, you have two solid choices in the Amazfit Bip 6 and Galaxy Fit 3.

#3309. ESR Black Friday gift guide: Premium accessories for iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, iPad, AirPods, and Apple Watch

If you picked up a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR says it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

On these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Why it matters: ESR says the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing shows up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Installation is the part most people dread on a brand-new iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and said it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

It’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR says it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

For the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

The trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the new M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

Have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

When the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR says the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

The result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

The ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

The ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

The best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the new iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. ESR’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run on Amazon from November 19 through November 30 (the Xtend 45W runs through December 1), with discounts of up to 37%!

Be sure to follow ESR on X and Facebook to keep up with all of its latest products, deals, and more.

#3306. Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. As you're adding item after item to your cart during the sale, you might be tempted by offers for an "affordable monthly payment system." Also known as "buy now, pay later" (BNPL), the pitch is a tempting one: Buy what you need now, and pay later, "on your own timeline." But as convenient as it sounds, you should think twice before using buy now, pay later options, whether during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or at any other time.

While BNPL plans can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any big discounts. Let's take a look at the hidden costs of BNPL, and why you're better off paying upfront for all your Black Friday purchases.

To be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the company is not uniquely misleading on this front. The process is straightforward: you choose your items, select Affirm (a third-party lender) at checkout, complete a quick application, and receive an instant decision on your loan terms. Individual transactions initiated through Affirm are limited to $25,000, with a daily maximum of $100,000 across multiple purchases—but of course, your Black Friday splurge will be nowhere near that big, right? (Right?!)

The main draw of these programs is the ability to "pay at your own pace." If you are required to pay a down payment, that is due at the time of the transaction. From there, your first monthly payment is usually due one month after your purchase is processed. Each following payment will be due one month later, on the same day of the month.

You can choose your own timeline, usually spanning 3, 6, 12, or 24 months, depending on the purchase amount and your creditworthiness. Unlike traditional credit cards, Affirm shows you the exact payment amount and total cost upfront, and claims no hidden fees or compound interest.

You need a separate Affirm account in addition to your Amazon Prime membership. The application process requires basic information, including your name, mobile phone number, date of birth, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Affirm performs a soft credit check initially, which doesn't impact your credit score, though they may conduct a hard inquiry for some loans.

BNPL plans are helpful if you really need to finance something big, but whenever possible, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses.

The ease of this sort of financing can make expensive purchases feel more affordable than they actually are. When you can buy a $1,000 tablet for "just $67 per month," it's easy to lose sight of the total cost, as well as your overall financial picture. In turn, this makes it all too easy to overspend on items you might not have purchased otherwise. You're better off taking a breath, stepping away from your shopping cart, and setting alerts to be notified when a product hits a price you can stomach, at a time you can afford it.

Despite what you may have heard in the past, BNPL providers may report to credit bureaus, meaning your BNPL purchases can in fact affect your credit score. For instance, all Affirm payments (including on-time, late, and missed payments) are now reported to the credit bureau Experian. So if you miss payments or default on the installment plan, it will cause damage to your credit score—making it even harder to get approved for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financing down the road.

Still, not all BNPL providers report to credit bureaus or use the same type of credit check, so it’s important to understand the specific terms and practices of any service you’re considering.

When you use a credit card, you get valuable purchase protections like extended warranty coverage, price protection, and the ability to dispute fraudulent charges. BNPL plans generally don't come with these safeguards. This means you're on the hook if something goes wrong with your BNPL purchase and the retailer doesn't make things right. The smarter move is to only buy what you can afford during a sale, no matter how tempting those deals may seem.

Although installment plans are helpful if you really need to finance something major, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses. Better to wait for a good price for something you truly need and can afford to pay for right now.

If there's a big-ticket item on sale for Black Friday but it's still out of your budget, consider these two questions before you turn to BNPL through Affirm:

Is this really an essential purchase? BNPL should really only be used on completely necessary purchases that you can’t afford right now, but can afford in six weeks. On that note...

Will I be able to pay this off within six weeks? When a bigger payment gets broken down into smaller installments, you might find yourself overspending in the long run, because it "feels" like you can afford it. Stay on top of how much you’re actually spending—especially if you're considering multiple BNPL purchases—and how it will impact your overall budget going forward.

For more information about deals and discounts, keep an eye on all of Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3303. Hulu’s 36-Episode Psychological Thriller Series Is Perfect From Start to Finish

With three Emmy wins for his role as Jesse Pinkman, Aaron Paul confirmed his pop culture icon status by starring in Breaking Bad. Even though Vince Gilligan initially intended to kill Jesse off, Paul’s inherent likability created the glue that held the AMC drama together. The actor earned his accolades as the traumatized meth cook who was just another victim of Walter White’s (Bryan Cranston). As iconic and dark as the role was, however, Paul followed up Breaking Bad with something even more harrowing.

After the conclusion of Breaking Bad, Paul starred in the Hulu series The Path. The show was set in an entirely different world than his previous one, but no less serious. Paul portrayed the role of Eddie Lane, an acolyte of the fictional Meyerist movement. The Path views this movement non-judgmentally, as the series is portrayed from the perspective of those in the cult. At its core, Meyerism is a self-help philosophy that draws on many real-life cults. Paul’s character is a heavily indoctrinated believer, along with his wife, Sarah (Michelle Monaghan), who grew up in the movement.

Only after going to a retreat does Eddie question his faith in Meyerism. As a convert, Eddie’s relationship with the so-called movement is shaken, but Sarah is much more stringent in her beliefs. This conflict leads to a dark character arc for Eddie, which rivals his role in Breaking Bad. A decade after its 2016 premiere, the 36-episode drama remains one of Paul’s more overlooked television performances.

Cults have been a source of fascination for a long time, but viewers won’t catch the actors saying such a thing about Meyerism. Michelle Monaghan, Aaron Paul, and Hugh Dancy, who plays a ranking official, Cal, were so immersed in the series' culture that they were reluctant to label the movement a cult.

“I could never call it a cult,” Dancy told E! News. “We are a movement. I think that’s relevant and that’s, in a way, the core of the show.” The far more interesting way to portray the series is to create it from the perspective of its acolytes and how insidious this type of thinking is. As Dancy says, no one in a cult thinks that they’re in a cult.

These ideas are prominent in many real-life movements, whether they are legally acknowledged as a cult or just a church. Regardless, Paul’s role in the series gets so close to reality that it can sometimes be uncomfortable. While on ayahuasca, Eddie receives a vision that leads him to believe there is no “Light,” a core tenet of Meyerism. His doubts lead to friction in the movement and eventually separation.

Called “deniers” in The Path, people who separate from these types of churches or movements are shunned by the community and often separated from their families. The Path shows what happens behind closed doors and the violence used as punishment. Ambition is also at the center of Meyerism as Cal becomes adversarial with Eddie. Cal is poised to become the next leader of Meyerism and has always been in love with Sarah. Considering Eddie’s controversial views, he is an easy target for Cal.

The Path is mostly disturbing because it shows the ramifications of boutique beliefs such as these. Though there are characters who want to dismantle such a system, Eddie goes through a harrowing character arc that doesn’t tie everything up in a bow. At least Jesse escapes his torment in a powerful Breaking Bad performance. The Path is even more morally ambiguous and questions everything the viewers have seen.

All 36 episodes across three seasons of The Path remain available to stream on Hulu in the U.S. as of November 2026.

#3302. How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can quickly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

Millions of Amazon Prime users currently pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other plans cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

Access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

For non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how quickly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

Also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's important to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching shows on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Of course, if you are interested in Prime Day bargains, you can always sign up right before the start of the sale and then cancel your membership after Prime Day is over—but Amazon doesn't always make it easy on you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. #3298. I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

With the recently launched Genie 4 update, this tool is purportedly even more powerful. It now allows you to request live edits (like "make it snow") and incorporate sound and dialog into your prompts. Google is also promising more realistic physics and natural movements in its renderings.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

It's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees."

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

The best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

That said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

#3295. ‘Yellowstone’ Meets ‘Desperate Housewives’ in Netflix’s Ambitious 2-Season Thriller

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Of all the things Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow) could have packed for her first night out in East Texas, the one that might have spared her a great deal of trouble was a sanitary pad. When a stranger asks her for one in the bathroom at an NRA fundraiser, Sophie offers a tampon, the stranger declines, and the two discover something they can agree on in Sophie’s purse. By the time they’ve each taken a Xanax, Sophie has made her first friend in Maple Brook. She’s also about to discover that the woman who just got half undressed in front of her is the wife of her husband’s boss.

There are any number of places The Hunting Wives could have introduced Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), including the stage where she joins her oil tycoon husband, Jed (Dermot Mulroney), as he floats the idea of running for governor. Having Sophie meet her in the bathroom first is considerably more fun. Everybody else at the party sees a prospective first lady of Texas. Sophie gets to spend the rest of the evening looking at that woman and thinking about what the two of them just did. Anybody who spent eight seasons of Desperate Housewives waiting for company to arrive at Bree Van de Kamp’s house at the worst possible moment should feel right at home. Adapted by Rebecca Cutter from May Cobb’s novel, The Hunting Wives has an eight-episode first season on Netflix and a second arriving on Thanksgiving Day, November 26. That gives you a perfectly respectable excuse to spend the long weekend with the Banks family, provided you’re prepared to explain what’s happening on the television when a relative wanders in.

John Dutton would understand Jed Banks just fine. One man made his name in Montana cattle country and the other made his in Texas oil, but both have spent enough time being the most important man in the room to figure they might as well be governor. What gives The Hunting Wives its own angle on familiar Yellowstone territory is where it sends Sophie once Jed finishes talking. Margo wants to know what she thought of his speech. Imagine being new in town, having exactly one professional connection through your husband, and discovering that his boss’s wife would like a little constructive criticism.

A look around Margo’s friend group explains how much is riding on her liking the answer. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) is married to the sheriff. Jill (Katie Lowes) is the pastor’s wife, and her son Brad (George Ferrier) is the local basketball star. Between them, these women have Sunday morning, Friday night, and any trouble you might get into in between pretty well covered. Most jealous friends have to settle for scrolling back to the beginning of your Instagram. When Callie catches on to Margo’s interest in Sophie, she has the resources of the sheriff’s office at her disposal.

Jill, meanwhile, can be perfectly sweet to Brad’s girlfriend, Abby (Madison Wolfe), while making it clear she thinks her son could do better. Lowes gets at something wonderfully aggravating about a mother who has promoted herself to the third person in a teenage relationship. You can imagine how Jill would describe the encounter to Brad afterward, and how ridiculous Abby would sound trying to explain what his mother did wrong. That’s where the Wisteria Lane resemblance runs deepest. Half the pleasure of watching these women misbehave comes from knowing whose side the neighbors would take if anybody complained.

Snow is funny in the early going because Sophie seems to share the audience’s judgment about everything happening around her, right up until Margo asks if she’d like to come along. There’s a lovely bit of cowardice in how long Sophie can pass off her interest as good manners. Going to the fundraiser was Graham’s idea, after all. Dinner with the Bankses could conceivably fall under the heading of supporting her husband’s career. Buying a pistol and leaving it at Margo’s place because Graham wouldn’t approve takes a little more explaining.

Åkerman makes Margo’s attention feel as good as Sophie thinks it does, even when we have an excellent view of the woman who was getting that attention yesterday. Early on, Margo offers Sophie a ride home from a bar, leaving a visibly disappointed Callie behind. You could spend the whole ride anticipating what might happen between the two women in the car, or you could spend it dying to get back to the bar to hear what Callie has to say. Even the woman who didn’t get invited along has a scene you want to see.

There is, of course, a murder to solve. The Hunting Wives opens with a girl running for her life before taking us back three weeks, and what makes those eight episodes go down so easily is how often you can forget about the shooting altogether. Jed and Margo have Sophie and Graham over for dinner, the hosts have rather different ideas about what’s on offer than their guests do, and suddenly the most pressing question in East Texas is how on earth these people are going to face each other at work on Monday.

#3294. Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company announced that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies plan to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.
